- A client names its batch as a `Store` mints it, `batch:<tag>:<n>` or `undo:<tag>:<n>` (`isClientBatch`); any other is refused `invalid`. A batch sent again is answered only with the asking seat's own ops, and one that holds somebody else's is refused `invalid`. A server mints its own batches outside that shape (`served:…`), and serves another seat's withheld op under an opaque `withheld:<16 hex>` batch. A `via` in a call or a post is a claim, ignored unless the host's `viaOf` accepts it (FR-52).
- The declaration `version` a welcome, a route and a `declaration` push say is the host's own monotonic number for the declaration it serves, the one a client hands `resolveApp`; a push with the number a client already serves is ignored.
- A declaration change is pushed as `declaration` (FR-43), and every welcome says the declaration `version` it serves. Neither moves `WIRE_PROTOCOL`.
- A host that holds the app read-only says so (FR-66): `{ t: "held", sentence }` to every socket that said hello when the hold starts, `sentence: null` when it ends, `held` in every welcome and on every answer a poll reads while it stands, and every change meanwhile refused `unavailable` in that sentence. Additive to protocol 1, so it does not move `WIRE_PROTOCOL` or the codec's name: a client that does not know the message ignores it.
- What a seat is served holds no id of a record it may not see (FR-55): not in the snapshot, the log, an op's primitives, inverse, reads, writes, call or sentence, a presence, a conflict, `/graview/health` or a tool's answer — beyond the seat's own words. A field whose current value this seat wrote (or the person an agent acts for; an undo is never the author of what it puts back) is served as written, whatever it names, and a record withheld only for such a field is served; so is the seat's own call in its own ops, and an argument it sent that an answer says back. A seat that guessed an id and wrote it is then served the same whether the guess was real, and a write of the value a field already holds, when that value names what the seat may not see, is kept in the log as the seat's. An oracle that checks what a seat is served excludes the strings the seat itself wrote. An act's sentence is worded from its author's view: `describe` reads the graph as the author is served it, so a record the author may not see is named only by what the author wrote, as one that does not exist is — and a reader who sees more reads that sentence as the author would have. The seat's own words excuse only what it wrote — values in its primitives and the inverse that puts them back, and its own calls; another author's call, sentence and name are judged by sight alone. An op records which records its sentence read (`described`), and another author's op is served whole only when its reader may see every one of them. An answer's `reads` name only records the seat sees; an id that names no record is left out as a hidden one is. `seatLens` is the judgment, and `seenBy`, `logSeenBy`, the routes, the live socket and the agent tools all read it. A seen record whose field names a hidden one is served with that field cleared when its kind declares the field optional (or does not declare it); when the field is required, clearing it would serve a record that fails its own declaration, so the record is withheld from that seat whole, as if its sight did not reach it — with its links, and with every op that touched it withheld. An op whose only mention of a hidden record is in its `reads` or `writes`, and whose primitives are served as written, is served whole with those trimmed. A link the seat is not served is no part of an op that did anything else: it is left out of the op's primitives and of its inverse, and the op is judged without it — so a removal that takes a record's links to what the seat may not see is served to the seat whole, as it would be had there been no such link, and the seat may undo it (the undo puts the links back, and is served to the seat the same way). An op that did nothing but such links is withheld. Any other op that names a hidden id is withheld, and its primitives are judged by whether each record was served just before and just after them: served to served is the patch as the seat is served the record (a hidden id written into an optional field arrives as that field cleared, `UNSET`); not served to served is an `add-node` of the record as now served, with its links to records the seat is served; served to not served is a `remove-node`; neither is nothing; and a link is served when both its ends are — an end that is not there at its moment, as a dangling link a repair removes has, is judged as `seesId` judges its id, so one that names no record is served and one that names a record the seat may not see, removed before, after or with the link, is not (FR-67). A seat from whom nothing is kept (`hidesFrom` false) is served every op as it is. So the log a seat is served folds — from nothing, from any cursor, or from the epoch base its view serves after a compaction — to exactly the snapshot it is served. `/graview/health` keeps `ok` and every count the whole store's — a poller asks whether the store is well, a count names no record, and a count of only what the asker sees would call a broken store well — and its `danglingEdges` names only the links whose ends the asking seat may be told of; a caller the host cannot tell is judged as a seat with no id and no roles. This narrows what a seat is sent and never adds a field, so it does not move `WIRE_PROTOCOL`.
- A sight may keep fields as well as records (Roadmap f-field-sight): `policy.sees[].hide` (field names it keeps) and `policy.sees[].fields` (the only field names it shows), both optional. A field of a record is shown to a seat when ANY sight that shows the seat that record shows the field — sights add up, `own` and `via` judged as for the record — so a sight with neither key shows every field. A field kept from a seat is never in anything it is served: the record (cleared, or the record withheld whole when its kind requires the field, as for a required reference), its log (an op that adds or removes a record with a kept field, writes one, or whose sentence read one is withheld whole whatever the field held, its primitives served as the seat is served the record; its own ops are served as it wrote them), an answer's diff and primitives, a conflict (a revision of a kept field is not compared or said), a search hit, a name a call resolves (a label is worked out from the served record), a form, an edit offered in place, a static page, a computed field (worked out over the served record) and a rule (judged over what the seat is served, so a kept field reads as none) — and nothing a seat reads differs between a kept field that holds a value and one that holds none. A seat may not write a field kept from it: an act that would is refused `invalid` as an argument it does not take ("does not take "phone"; it takes …"), asked before a write of the value the field holds is let go as no change, so the refusal is the same whatever it held and whatever was written; a kept field an act leaves unset is no write. An import refuses a column that goes to a kept field exactly as one that goes to no field. An op's `described` may name `<id>#<field>` for each field of a record of a kind some sight keeps fields of that its sentence read. Judging fields is `@graview/core/field-sight`'s; until it is loaded, a sight with `hide` or `fields` shows nothing — the store keeps the record rather than serve a field it cannot judge, and says the seat neither sees every record of the kind nor, when it may begin none, the kind at all (`kindsKeptFrom`) — except in a store `openRemote` opened, which shows what its host served it: that store alone (`FIELD_SIGHT.served`), never another store the same page holds whole. An agent's tool for an act leaves out each argument that writes a field no sight granting the seat that kind shows on any record (`argumentsNeverShown`, `@graview/core/json-schema`), so the tool names no field the seat may not see, and `toolDefinitions` says the same surface without a store. `@graview/ship`'s server entry loads it; a page that holds its whole store (`openStore` from `@graview/ship/browser`, or a `Store` of its own) imports it, as does a host that serves seats without `@graview/ship`. A build before 0.1.29 ignores both keys and shows the field: a host serves a declaration that says either only on a build that exports `FIELD_SIGHT` from `@graview/core`.
- An act may touch what its seat cannot see (FR-55), and `replaces` (FR-115) is such an act by design. Before it connects, it severs the subject's links of the relations it names, all but the one it makes — whatever record is on the far end, seen or not — exactly as connecting a cardinality-one relation severs the link it displaces. A seat that moves a component to a new owner may so cut its link to an owner it may not see. That is the policy, not a leak: the seat is served the severed link as nothing (a link is served only when both its ends are), the op as its primitives are judged above, and an agent tool's answer the same way, so the act changes what the seat cannot see without telling it what was there. An installation that must not let a seat displace a hidden record says so in the act's condition or its grants, not by relying on sight.
- A status board's moves (FR-108) are judged against the graph the page holds, and the host judges them under the seat's sight. On a served app the page holds the seat's view, so a named step whose condition reads a record the seat may not see is judged without it on the page and at the host alike: a step is offered exactly when the host would run it, and run when offered. Nothing tells the seat what it cannot see, and nothing moves `WIRE_PROTOCOL`.
- A host's files (FR-163) are a seam on the page, `files: { upload(file, name), maxBytes, kinds }` on `mount`, `<Embed>`, `GraviewProvider`, the Shell and the routed face's context, and the route that serves them is the host's own; within a major the seam's three members keep their meaning, and the value `upload` answers is a `FileValue` (FR-162) the record keeps as it is. What the route serves is part of the app's origin, and the page draws it as such: a picture in an `<img>`, which never runs a script, an SVG's included; a PDF in an `<object>`, which draws whatever type the route answers with; anything else as a link with `download`. So a host's files route: serves each file as the type the host decided from its bytes, never the type the uploader said, with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`; sends `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox` with everything but a PDF (an SVG or an HTML file opened from it, in a tab or in that `<object>`, runs as the app otherwise), and with a PDF where its readers' browsers draw one sandboxed; says `Content-Disposition: attachment` for anything that is not a picture, a PDF or plain text; and serves a file only to a seat that sees a record holding it, the framework's sight being per record (`seesId(store, principal)` over the records whose fields hold the `href`, by `filesOf`). The dev door (`devFiles`, `@graview/ship/dev`) does the rest but the first and the last: it keeps the type it was sent, which under `nosniff` and the sandbox runs nothing, and every seat on a dev server is its one person. A host's page that carries a `Content-Security-Policy` allows the files route in `object-src` (`'self'`, or the files origin) if it wants a PDF drawn inline; where it does not, or where the browser draws no PDF (an iPhone), the page draws the PDF's one line — its name, its type, its size, Open and Download — and the `<object>` takes its height only once the browser has loaded the PDF into it, so nothing is lost and no empty box is drawn (FR-234).
- A host's way to name another app (FR-171) is a seam on the page, `resolveApp(address, viewer)` on `mount`, `<Embed>`, `GraviewProvider`, the `Shell` (asked before the provider's) and the routed face's context, answering `{ name, icon?, headline?, href }`, `{ denied: true }` or `null`; within a major those three answers keep their meaning. The page asks once per address and viewer and remembers the answer for as long as it holds that resolver; a throw is taken as `null`. A viewer the host refuses is shown "linked app (no access)" and nothing the host did not answer, so whether another app exists, what it is called and what its home says stay the host's to tell each viewer. Without a resolver the address is drawn as it is kept, a link only when it is an absolute http(s) address, opened apart from the app (`rel="noopener noreferrer"`). `href` is followed only when it is a path on the host or an http(s) address.
- A host's way to read another app's records (FR-171) is a seam beside it, `linkedRecords: LinkedRecords` on `mount`, `<Embed>`, `GraviewProvider` and the routed face's context: `resolve(ref, viewer)` with `ref` `{ address, kind, id }`, answering `{ address, kind, id, label, describe?, card?, fields, href?, app? }` (`fields` only what that viewer may see there), `{ denied: true }`, or `null`; `find({ address, kinds, query, limit }, viewer)`, answering the records that viewer may link or `{ denied: true }`; and `open(ref, viewer)`, optional, the navigation seam a press on a linked record calls in place of following its `href`. Within a major those answers keep their meaning. A page asks once per record and viewer; a throw is `null`. A viewer refused is shown "linked record (no access)" and nothing the host did not answer. `href` is followed only when it is a path on the host or an http(s) address. `linkedRecordsOver` (`@graview/core/linked`) is that seam over stores a host holds in memory, each record read through the far store's `seenBy(viewer)`; `recordLinkedChange(store, { ref, fields, app?, at? })` keeps a far change in the reading store's history as an ordinary op — author `{ kind: "system", id: "app:<address>", name }`, `via: "app:<address>"`, `reads` the linking records, no primitives, no new op field, naming the fields that changed and none of their values.
- A worker view's manifest and what it is handed are held to the guest protocol's rules: a key may be added when it is optional and a manifest without it means what it meant; a build that predates a key passes it over (one before 0.1.18 draws a view with `replaces` as it drew every view of one: alone). `replaces` arrived this way (FR-149): `"page"` on a view of one record draws it alone in place of the record's own fields, and `checkManifest` refuses any other value and the key on a view of the home. Since FR-203 a view of many may say it too, and is then drawn on its kind's list page (`/<plural>`) in place of the list, a titled one at its own place as well; before, `checkManifest` refused it there, so no manifest that worked reads differently, and an earlier build refuses it. What a view of one record replaces changed without the manifest's text: since FR-149 a view of one is drawn above the record's own editable fields on the scene (on Pages it always was), where it was drawn alone; a host that relied on the record being the view alone adds `replaces: "page"`. `data-prefill` (FR-150) is an attribute a view draws, judged by the host: it fills only an empty `input` or `textarea` whose `name` is the field, from a record the view was shown, read through the viewer's sight, when an act in its `fieldset` named in the manifest writes that field of that record and the viewer may run it there; a press carries the value only back into that field, and any other press carrying it is refused `untyped`. A view's props are as they were: each record's fields on it by name, beside `id`, `kind` and `label` (FR-151 corrected the guide, not the props). `GUEST_PROTOCOL` does not move.

##### Refusal codes are open (1.0)

- A code may be added within a major; none is removed or changes meaning. A client that meets a code it does not know treats it as a final refusal: the change is taken back and the refusal handed on with the code as it came (`openRemote`'s `onRefusal`, `RemoteRefusedError`), never kept and sent again as `unavailable` is. A program that branches on codes keeps a default for the rest.
- `unauthenticated` (1.0's foundation): the host does not know who is asking — no session, or one that ran out — and signing in again may let the same change through. 401 over HTTP.
- `quota` (1.0's foundation): the account the app belongs to has used what its plan allows; the change may succeed once the allowance grows, never by waiting. 403 over HTTP.
- A host says either, and `limit`, as its own final refusal: its `limit` or `admit` answers `{ refuse, reason }` (`HostRefusalReason`; `limit`, 413, when it names none). A body too large to take is `limit`; a caller sending too much too fast is told `busy` with a wait, which is not a refusal. Neither needed a code of its own.

##### Served state and the head

What a seat is served is the app as this seat is served it, and nothing on any surface promises that is the store's head. FR-55 narrows what a seat is served by record and by field; a seat's served state may also end before the head, at a seq a policy chooses, and that is narrowing by seq — the same kind of change, not a break — so it moves neither `WIRE_PROTOCOL` nor any format.

- A seat is served through a seq, `servedSeq`: the ops before it are in what it reads, none after. `Store.servedSeq` says it, read-only: a store's own is its head (`log.length`), a past's (`pastOf(store, seq)`) is `seq`, and a seat's view (`seenBy`) is the seq that seat is served through. Every seat of a live app is served through the head; a reader of an app that publishes is served through the last publish (below).
- `GET /graview/since?seq=<cursor>` answers the ops after the cursor that the asking seat is served — through its served seq, which is the head unless a policy holds it behind — not necessarily every op to the head, and the cursor where they leave it. The live socket's positions mean the same: `welcome.seq` is where the seat stands in what it is served, and `ops` brings what the seat is served as it lands. A client that takes a position for the head's takes it for the seat's (below, *A cursor is opaque*).
- `seenBy`, `Store.seenBy`, a provider's `store`, `useGraph`, an agent's reads and a seat's model prompt read the app as the seat is served it. Their doc comments say so and promise neither the head nor one view object per principal: the view is kept only to save judging again, keyed by everything serving reads (the seat's kind, the id and roles it is judged as, the agent's own id when it acts for somebody — two agents for one person are two seats — and where it is served through).
- A write is always judged at the head, whatever the seat is served. A call's stale-write check (`base`, FR-05) reads the head's revisions: a seat served behind the head that claims the revision it read is not stale unless the field was written after that revision, and when it was, the conflict says the head's value.
- A client whose seq the ops cannot catch up is sent the whole state, never the ops after a gap: a socket's `hello` whose seq is behind the compaction horizon, or past where its seat is now served, is answered with a `welcome` carrying `state` (and such a `welcome` may come unasked when a publish is taken back); `/graview/since` answers such a seq with `reset: true` — and, behind the horizon, the ops after it, so a client that predates `reset` still sees the gap. `openRemote` takes the state on either.
- A checkpoint never passes a seq somebody is served at. `CompactOptions.pins` (`store.checkpoint`, ship's `opened.compact`) are such seqs, and the horizon stops at the lowest, so `pastOf(store, pin)` still folds from the log. A host that serves a seat behind the head passes that seq.
- **Publishing** (Roadmap f-publishing-lifecycle). A declaration's `publishing` (`{ mode: "live" | "on-publish", working: [roles], publishers?: [roles] }`, the document's key and `defineApp`'s alike, `StoreOptions.publishing` on the store) says when edits reach readers. `"live"`, or absent, is every app as it was. Under `"on-publish"` a seat whose roles (an agent's read through the person it acts for) are `working` is served the head, and every other seat — a visitor, an embed, a static page, another app's linked read, a describe for a reader — is served `pastOf(store, publishedSeq)` as its sight reaches it; before the first publish, the log's start (the seed, or the horizon of a log compacted past it). `seenBy(principal, { as: "published" })`, a provider's `as` and `?as=published` serve a collaborator what readers are served, to preview it. Writes land on the head whoever makes them: a visitor's form answer is in the working state, and reaches readers with the next publish. A publish is the built-in act `publish` (`{ through? }`), offered to `publishers` (absent, `working`): one op authored by the person who published, with no primitives and the op field `publishedThrough` — the seq readers are served through, its own seq + 1 unless `through` names an earlier one. The last publish op that stands says it (`Store.publishedSeq`), so taking a publish back is an undo of it, permitted to publishers. How a reader is served, the `publish` act and the published seq are `@graview/core/publishing`'s, an entry of its own so a live app's page carries none of it: a server, a static page, a linked read and the agent tools load it, a page fetches it with `@graview/core/past` before it draws an app that publishes, and until it is loaded a reader of such an app is refused — never served the head. A checkpoint keeps the app as it stood at each published seq behind it that readers are or may again be served (`Epoch.published`, a list of epochs; also `Epoch.publishedThrough`, what stood published at its seq), so a compaction passes old publishes, a reader is served one behind the horizon from it, and only before the first publish is the horizon held, at where the log begins. Both are optional and additive within format 1: a checkpoint without `published` serves readers what the log folds and refuses an undo of a publish that would send them behind the horizon. A store whose checkpoint carries `published` is snapshot format 2 (§2), so a build that predates `published` refuses it rather than serve its readers the horizon; a host that must roll back to such a build compacts with `format: 1`, which holds the horizon at the earliest seq readers are served behind it and says where it stopped (a pin at `store.publishedSeq` alone does not: a horizon between two publishes is format 2 with it). Neither is served to a seat. On the wire, a reader's `welcome`, `/graview/state` and `/graview/since` carry `servedThrough`, a cursor as opaque as any other position (below, *A cursor is opaque*), absent in a live app, its socket is sent the ops between two publishes when the second lands, and the whole state when a publish is taken back. A build that predates publishing folds an op carrying `publishedThrough` as it would without it (a marker that touches nothing) and refuses the document key by path (§4) — the fail-closed way back: an app that publishes is never opened by a build that would serve its readers the head. Named by no FR id yet: `capabilities().shipped` gains one when Graview Cloud files it.

##### A cursor is opaque (1.0)

Where a reader stands in a log is said on the wire as a cursor: a string only the server that gave it reads, meaningful to no other server and to no other store on the same one. A store keeps numbering its ops, and an op's own `seq` is unchanged; what moved is every position a client and a server say to each other, so a server that one day merges several writers' logs can say where a reader stands without one sequence.

- **Where it is said.** `GET /graview/since?seq=<cursor>` takes one and answers `cursor`, where its ops leave the reader; `GET /graview/state` answers `cursor`; `POST /graview/here` takes `seq` and answers `cursor` beside its ops; the socket's `hello` says `seq`, and its `welcome`, `ack` and `ops` say `seq` (`Cursor`, `@graview/ship`).
- **What a client may do with it.** Keep the last one it was given and send it back. It must not read one, build one from an op's `seq`, or compare two. `openRemote` speaks the same build's codec as the server it was built with (`cursorAt`), and a cursor today is `s` and a count in base 36 — which is this build's business, not a promise: a server may change what is inside within a major.
- **A page from before it** (0.1.48 and earlier) sends the seq of the last op it has, a number. A server reads that, and a numeric string, as before for one minor (`seqAt`), and stops in the minor after; such a page reads nothing it is sent as a number, so the tokens in a `welcome`, an `ack` and an `ops` message do not disturb it. A seq a server can read as neither is refused `invalid` (400).
- `SyncState.cursor` was a remote system's own string from the start and is held to the same rule: the engine keeps it and hands it back, and never reads it.

#### 4. The declaration, the document format and check finding codes

A declaration that compiled and checked clean on one version compiles on the next version of the major.

- A check finding's `code` never changes meaning. A new code may appear, and a new warning or note is not a break. A new *error* on a declaration that used to pass is a break.
- A code that only ever said again what another code says may be retired, and the changelog says so. `act-without-title` was retired this way: a mutation without a title was reported twice, as that warning and as the error `mutation-untitled`, which names the path and the fix and is the one finding now. A program that matched on the retired code matches on `mutation-untitled`.
- The stored-data finding codes of `validateGraph` (FR-21) hold to the same rule. Each is a record, a link or a rule that no longer fits the declaration, found by id:

| Code | What it says | `repairPlan` | |------|--------------|--------------| | `node-shape` | a record's field does not fit its kind (`detail` names the field) | clear an optional field, coerce a required one to its default, else drop the record with its links | | `kind-unknown` | a record of a kind the declaration no longer has | drop it, with its links | | `edge-dangling` | a link to or from a record that is not there | drop the link | | `edge-disallowed` | a link the declaration does not allow between those kinds | drop the link | | `rule-error` | a rule threw rather than judged (`could-not-judge`; `detail` names the rule) | none: the declaration's to fix | | `rule-budget` | a rule would have read more than its budget (`over-budget`) | none: the declaration's to fix |

- The declaration document format (FR-01) is versioned like a stored format, and `capabilities().documentFormats` lists what a build parses.
- A key may be added to a document format within its version when it is optional and a document without it means what it meant: `kinds.<kind>.computed` (FR-83) arrived in `graview-document@1` this way. Every key is closed, so a build that predates one refuses a document that uses it as `unknown-key`, by path, and never misreads it. A host that keeps documents for more than one build reads `capabilities().shipped` before it writes the key.
- The app's money arrived the same way (FR-100). Its one home is the brand: `brand.currency` (a three-letter code) and `brand.locale` (a language tag) in a document, `Brand.currency` and `Brand.locale` in a declaration, and a document's `brand` may now carry them without an `accent`. A figure or a field shown as money takes `currency` of its own; one that names none, and a template's `{x | money}`, take the brand's, written by `Intl.NumberFormat` in the brand's locale ("en-US" when it names none). A document without them says a sum as it always did: a figure with a currency in that currency, anything else as a number with no symbol. A figure's and a meter's `label` became a template (FR-99): a label without braces says what it said. The rule language gained `out(S, 'edge')`, `in(S, 'edge')` and `&`, `|` and `-` between sets (FR-101); an expression that parsed before means what it meant, except that a `|` inside brackets within a template's braces, which was a formatter and refused, is now a join. A build that predates them refuses `brand.currency`, `brand.locale`, a field's `currency` and a set operator by path, but draws a templated label as its words and a two-argument walk as "—", so a host reads `capabilities().shipped` for FR-99, FR-100 and FR-101 before it writes them.
- A number's range arrived the same way (FR-114): `min`, `max` and `step` on a `number` or `integer` field (and on an act's declared argument), each optional, a field without them taking any number as before. The edit vocabulary gained `set-range`, and `DocumentDiff` gained `narrowedRanges`. A range is judged by the checker (`default-range`, `field-range`), not by `readDocument`. A build that predates them refuses the keys by path, so a host reads `capabilities().shipped` for FR-114 before it writes them.
- An act's `setsOther` and `replaces` arrived the same way (FR-115), each optional, an act without them doing what it did. One meaning changed with them: an act's `connects` or `severs` shorthand on a subject that is only the far end of the relation (`connects: "owns"` on a component, where `owns` is declared on person) now links from the record it is given to the subject, as the declaration says the relation goes; before, it tried the link the other way round, which the graph refused, so no document that worked reads differently. `effectsOf` may return a `ReplaceEffect` beside the effects a document lists. A host reads `capabilities().shipped` for FR-115 before it writes the keys.
- The rest of the brand arrived the same way (FR-124): `brand.logo` (inline SVG, or a path under `/graview/assets/` or relative to the page; a string, or `{ "src", "alt" }`), `brand.favicon` (the same forms), `brand.typography` (`display`, `body`, `mono`: `system-serif`, `system-sans`, `system-mono`, or a stack of faces every system has and the web fonts on `DOCUMENT_FONTS`), `brand.shape` (`radius` 0–32, `density` 0.75–1.5), `brand.accents` (a hue per kind) and `brand.scheme` (`light`, `dark` or `auto`), each optional and each mapped onto the TypeScript `Brand` (which gains `logoAlt`, `favicon`, `subtitle` and `scheme`). A document's `description` is now said on both faces — the app name's hover on the app bar and the line on the routed face's home (FR-131) — and every document compiles to a brand, so a document without one is called by its own `name` where it was called Graview. The checker judges the new keys (`brand-mark`, `brand-font` errors; `brand-accent` a warning about an accent that does not read as given, FR-126). The edit vocabulary gained `set-name` and `set-description`, and `set-brand` takes every key, `null` clearing one; `DocumentDiff`'s sentences for the name and the description changed words ("The app is now called…"). A build that predates them refuses the keys by path, so a host reads `capabilities().shipped` for FR-124 and FR-125 before it writes them. A compiled app carries the new keys in its `brand` within `graview-compiled@1`: a page that predates them draws the brand it knows.
- A logo for each scheme arrived the same way, in 0.1.42, and was named FR-197 in 0.1.44: `brand.logo` as `{ "light", "dark"?, "alt"?, "darkFallback"?: "invert" }` beside the string and `{ "src", "alt" }`, which mean what they meant. A build before 0.1.42 refuses the object by path (`brand.logo`), so a host stores a document whose logo has `light` only on a build whose `capabilities().shipped` names FR-197 — a build of 0.1.42 or 0.1.43 holds the form but does not say so. `logoOfDocument` on `@graview/core/document` reads any of the three forms into `{ light, dark?, alt?, darkFallback? }`.
- A compiled app (FR-123) is versioned like a stored format. It is what a host hands its page so the page need not compile: `serializeCompiled(compileDocument(document))`, plain JSON with every template and expression already parsed, which `appFrom` (from `@graview/core/compiled`) builds into the same app `compileDocument` made. It says `"format": "graview-compiled@1"`. `appFrom` refuses another format as `compiled-format`, by name, and parts that do not match their document as `compiled-shape`, and never misreads either; `appFromOrCompile` then compiles the document in the page, so a compiled app cached from another build costs one request, not a broken page. It does the same for one torn on its way (refused `compiled-shape`, never thrown) and for one compiled from another document than the one handed beside it — two documents are the same when their canonical text is (`canonicalize`), so a host hands the document the compiled app was made from, in the current document format. Within a version the format is additive: a key an older page ignores, and a page that lacks it can do without, may be added. Anything a page would need to build the same app moves the version: a new effect, a new kind of argument, a change to what a parsed expression or template part holds. So the rule language's tree (`Expr`) and `TemplatePart` are part of this format, and a parser change that alters them is a format change. A compiled app is a cache of its document, never its source. A host keeps the document, compiles it at its own build, and may drop a compiled app at any time. It is the host's own data, checked for its format and shape and not judged again.
- A check finding code added this way (FR-99's `view-braces`, FR-100's `brand-currency` and `brand-locale`, FR-105's `act-reads-hidden-kind`, FR-108's `lens-column-unreached`, FR-114's `default-range` and `field-range`, FR-115's `act-sets-other` and `act-replaces`, FR-124's `brand-mark` and `brand-font`, FR-126's `brand-accent`, FR-132's `pages-overview-taken`, FR-137's `pages-faces-alike`, FR-148's `page-field`, `page-field-twice`, `page-group-twice`, `page-unknown-field` and `page-too-large`, 0.1.24's `rule-says-hidden-fact`, 0.1.60's `typing-act-without-allowed-on`, and FR-232's `face-reads-content-beside-the-graph`, which `graview check` says of a project's face modules and no declaration or document ever meets) is a warning, a note or an error only about what is new: `act-reads-hidden-kind`, `rule-says-hidden-fact`, `typing-act-without-allowed-on`, `face-reads-content-beside-the-graph` and `view-braces` are warnings, `lens-column-unreached` is a note, and the brand, range, other-end and page codes judge keys a declaration could not hold before.
- The scene's name arrived the same way (FR-132), and its key was respelled when the scene left the places for the bar's switch (FR-137): `pages.scene` and `pages.pages` (at most 40 characters each, as `pages.overview` was) are what the switch calls the two faces, "Scene" and "Pages" when unsaid, and `arrange-pages` takes `scene` and `pages`. The scene keeps the address `/places/overview` whatever it is called. `pages.overview`, which named the scene's tab in 0.1.15 and 0.1.16, is read as `pages.scene` (a line in `RESPELLED`), so a stored document keeps its word, and `arrange-pages` still reads `overview` as `scene`, so a chat or a tool written before 0.1.17 still renames the scene. `pages-faces-alike` is a warning about a declaration whose two words are the same. `pages-overview-taken` is a warning about a declared place whose address is the scene's; that place keeps its page on the routed face, and the place list does not offer it. A build that predates the keys passes them over.
- Where a declaration opens changed without its text (FR-136): an app with a home view (the document's `views.home`, or a worker view attached to `"home"`) and no other `pages.first` opens on Pages at its home when the host names no face, where it opened on the scene, and `placesOf` marks the home `first`. Under address routing the bare address, naming no face, is the home's whatever face the host names, and the host is told the pages (`onFace`). A host that wants the scene there links to `/places/overview`, or hands a stop. An app without a home view opens as before. That address alone is the overview at altitude (FR-154): a fragment never reaches a server, so the framework writes the overview at altitude without one, and reads `/places/overview` with no fragment, or one that says nothing, as at altitude; a fragment that says where it stands (`#focus=t1`, `#overview=1&focus=…`) is read as it says, and `#overview=1`, written before, still opens it.
- A kind's page arrived the same way (FR-148): `kinds.<kind>.page`, `{ "fields": [...], "groups": [{ "title", "fields" }] }`, each part optional, says which facts a record's page shows first and under which headings; the rest follow in the kind's declared order, under "Details" when there are groups. The declaration's `display.page` is the same choice. The edit vocabulary gained `set-page-fields` (`{ kind, fields, groups? }`; an empty `fields` and no `groups` take the choice away), and the compile and `graview check` refuse a name the kind does not have or one named twice (`page-field`, `page-field-twice`, `page-group-twice` in a document; `page-unknown-field` and `page-field-twice` in TypeScript). A build that predates the key refuses it as `unknown-key`. One reading changed without a key: a record's facts are read in the kind's declared order on every face, in `describePlace` and in `readableFields`, where they were read in the order the record's own keys were written.
- A document's facts and a kind's roles arrived the same way, with no FR id (0.1.22). The document's top-level `computed` names facts of the whole graph, each a rule-language expression or `{ "expr", "label" }`, read as `fact('<name>')` wherever the language is read; a fact that reads another in a circle is refused (`computed-cycle`). `kinds.<kind>.fieldRoles` says which field fills a role a lens binds by name, and the framework reads two: `when` (a date; a list of the kind opens newest first by it, and a timeline or calendar draws the kind there) and `who` (a name; an unchosen glance leads with it and `when`); `graview check` refuses a role naming no field (`field-role-missing-field`) or of the wrong type (`field-role-ill-typed`). A kind may word its own end of a relation several kinds declare, so `edge-name-shared` is no longer reported. A build that predates the keys refuses them by path. These carry no FR id, so `capabilities().shipped` cannot announce them, and `capabilities()` does not list document keys: it is on every page's first load, and the keys a build reads are already published with it, as `@graview/core/document.schema.json` (JSON Schema, one per version). A host that writes a document for more than one build validates it against the schema of the oldest build it serves, or lets `readDocument` there refuse it by path.
- A picture or a document on a record arrived the same way (FR-162): the field types `image` and `file`, and `list` with `of: "image"` or `of: "file"`, in a document; `imageField()` and `fileField()` in a declaration, which `toDocument` writes as those types. The value is a `FileValue`, `{ href, name, type, bytes, width?, height?, caption? }`, its `href` a path on the host under its base (`/graview/files/3f9a….jpg`, or one relative to the page) and never a scheme, another host, a backslash or a path that climbs (`safeFileHref`); a store refuses any other value as it refuses any value that does not fit its field. A view's blocks gained `{ "image": "<field>", "as": "thumb" | "gallery", "label"? }`, judged by the check (`view-image`, an error about a block that could not be written before, and `view-format` for its `as`). `graview types` writes such a field as `FileValue` (or `readonly FileValue[]`). A build that predates them refuses the types and the block by path, so a host reads `capabilities().shipped` for FR-162 before it writes them. A compiled app carries the new field types within `graview-compiled@1`: a page that predates them cannot build such a field, refuses the compiled app as `compiled-shape` and compiles the document, which refuses the type by path. A change that leaves no record holding a file says so: `MigrationPlan.files` lists them, and the plan's words name them; what becomes of their bytes is the host's to decide.
- A link to another app arrived the same way (FR-171): the field type `app-link` in a document, `appLinkField()` in a declaration, which `toDocument` writes as that type. The value is another app's address — `@owner/app`, an id its host knows it by, or an absolute http(s) address, at most 500 characters (`isAppAddress`) — and a store refuses any other value as it refuses any value that does not fit its field. `graview types` writes it as `string`. A build that predates it refuses the type by path, so a host reads `capabilities().shipped` for FR-171 before it writes one; a compiled app carries it within `graview-compiled@1`, and a page that predates it refuses the compiled app as `compiled-shape` and compiles the document, which refuses the type by path. A relation whose `to` is another app's kind is the next line.
- A relation to a kind in another app arrived the same way (FR-171, the full relation): a relation's `to` may name `"@<app address>/<kind>"` — `"@nick/house/house"`, `"@app_kf5eydr9z58jzf/house"`, `"@https://example.com/a/house/house"` — every target one app's kind (`parseLinkedTarget`; the address is the one an app-link holds), and `linkedRecordField("@nick/house/house", { cardinality? })` in a declaration, which `toDocument` writes as that relation. The record that links keeps which far record as a value under the relation's name, `"<kind>:<id>"` (`linkedValue`), or a list of them for `"many"`; the far document is never written. `graview check` refuses a relation that mixes this app's kinds with another's (`linked-mixed`), reaches two apps (`linked-apps`), is no app's kind (`linked-target`), or says `inverse` (`linked-inverse`) or `appendOnly` (`linked-append-only`), a declared act that connects, severs or sets one (`act-linked`), and a rule that walks one with `out()` or `in()` (`rule-linked`); a page that compiles without the checker reads such a relation as no relation. The rule language walks it by name (`forHouse.listPrice`) through the reader of whoever is looking: a far record it cannot read, refused or not yet answered, reads as nothing and is said — a computed value's `refused` sentence, a rule `could-not-judge` where it would not hold without it — never thrown. `graview types` writes it as `string` (or `readonly string[]`). A build that predates it refuses an `@` target by path, so a host reads `capabilities().shipped` for FR-171 before it writes one; a compiled app carries it within `graview-compiled@1`. Since 0.1.35 the edit `add-relation` takes such a `to` too, judged by the same rules and refused with the same codes at `edits.<n>`, and said as `scenario gains a relation, "forHouse", to one house in the app @nick/house, another app, read there as whoever is looking.`; `rename-relation` and `remove-relation` work on one, and `planMigration` keeps its values, moves them with a rename and clears them with the relation.
- A phone, a place and a length of time arrived the same way, with no FR id (the Graview Roadmap's f-more-field-types): the field types `phone`, `place` and `duration` in a document, `phoneField()`, `placeField()` and `durationField()` in a declaration, which `toDocument` writes as those types. A phone is a string of at most 40 characters with at least three digits and only the spaces, `+`, `-`, `.`, `/`, parentheses and extension (`ext. 12`, `x12`) people write one with (`PHONE`); a place a string of at most 500; a duration a whole number of minutes, none less than none, which a duration field's `min`, `max` and `step` bound as a number's do (FR-114). A store refuses any other value as it refuses any value that does not fit its field. How each is said and linked is the page's and may change in a minor: a phone grouped as a reader in the US or Canada reads a North American number and as entered elsewhere, linked `tel:`; a place linked to maps.apple.com on Apple's platforms and Google's universal Maps address elsewhere, opened apart (`rel="noopener noreferrer"`); a duration said "1 h 30 min", and so is a computed field that says `as: "duration"` — which a TypeScript declaration says itself, and a document's compile writes for each computed field whose parsed expression adds, subtracts, negates or sums durations over a relation (`KindPlan.durations` in `graview-compiled@1`, optional; a face reads only `as`, never the expression's words). `graview types` writes a phone and a place as `string` and a duration as `number`. A build that predates them refuses the types by path; these carry no FR id, so a host validates a document that uses them against the `document.schema.json` of the oldest build it serves. A compiled app carries them within `graview-compiled@1`: a page that predates them cannot build such a field, refuses the compiled app as `compiled-shape` and compiles the document, which refuses the type by path.
- Markdown in a text field arrived the same way (FR-180): `"format": "markdown"` on a document's `text` field, `markdownField()` in a declaration (a string of at most 20,000 characters, marked so `isMarkdownField`, from `@graview/core/words`, says so through optional, default and nullable), which `toDocument` writes as that format. The value is kept as written. `retype-field` takes `"format": "markdown"` to make a text field Markdown and drops it when left out; `diffDocuments` says either change and neither is breaking. The checker refuses `markdown` on any type but `text`, and a number's format on a `text`, as `field-format`. A build that predates it refuses the format by path, so a host reads `capabilities().shipped` for FR-180 before it writes one; a compiled app carries it within `graview-compiled@1`. The record's page draws it as prose through `@graview/core/markdown` — headings demoted under the page's own, paragraphs with their line breaks kept, lists, emphasis, code, quotations, rules and tables, links only to `http:`, `https:` and `mailto:` (`rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow"`, a new tab), a picture as its words, and no HTML: within a major that reading only grows, and nothing it reads ever becomes markup. A row, a card, a describe line, a table cell, a search hit and a seat's line about a record say a text field by its start (`excerptOf`, from `@graview/core/words`): its first paragraph, heading or item, or about 160 characters, Markdown's syntax taken out; the exact words may be tuned within a major.
- Whether a field is typed together arrived the same way (collaborative text, phase 2): a document's field may say `"collaborative": true | false`, which only a `text` or a `string` field takes — the checker refuses it on any other type as the error `field-collaborative`, on a key a build before it refused by path anyway — and unsaid, a `text` field is typed together and a `string` is not. `toDocument` writes the key only where a declaration marked a field (`markCollaborative`) against what its type says by default. `graview describe` says which fields are typed together.
- A date that repeats arrived the same way, with no FR id (0.1.29, the Roadmap's f-recurring-dates): `"repeats": true` on a `date` or `datetime` field in a document, `repeatField()` beside the date in a declaration (`startsAtRepeat: repeatField()` beside `startsAt`), which `toDocument` writes as `repeats`. A record of the kind may keep, under the date's name and `Repeat`, `{ "every": "day" | "week" | "month" | "year", "interval"?: 1–99, "on"?: weekdays ("tue") for a week or days of the month (1–31, -1 the last) for a month, "until"?: a day, "count"?: 1–1000, "except"?: days, "continues"?: a record's id }`, or `null` once it no longer repeats; the date itself is the first occurrence, and a store refuses any other value (`validRepeat`). The key `<date>Repeat` is the framework's: a kind that has a field, relation or computed field of that name is refused (`repeat-clash`). Occurrences are worked out, never stored, and what reads the date reads the occurrence on or after the day it is judged on — the rule language, `today()`'s comparisons, a template, a list's sort, filter and date groups, and a kind's "in the next 7 days" — so a rule over a repeating date is judged anew when the day turns (FR-176) with nothing written. A day the series falls on that the month lacks (the 31st, Feb 29) is the month's last; a moment's time of day is kept as written, so one written without a zone stays at its wall time across a clock change and one written with a zone keeps that offset; `count` counts skipped days. Time zones beyond the one a moment says, and the rest of RFC 5545 (by-week-number, by-set-position, hourly), are not this. The edit vocabulary gained `set-repeats` (`{ kind, field, repeats }`, refused of a field that is not a date); `retype-field` away from a date lets `repeats` go; a migration moves a record's repeat with its date when the date is renamed, and a change that stops a date repeating drops each record's repeat and says so (`DocumentDiff` counts `<date>Repeat` among `removedFields`, so it is breaking). `graview types` writes `<date>Repeat?: Repeat | null`. A build that predates it refuses `repeats` as `unknown-key`, and a compiled app carries it within `graview-compiled@1`; a page that predates it refuses such a compiled app as `compiled-shape` and compiles the document, which refuses the key by path, so a host that writes `repeats` serves builds of 0.1.29 or later. These carry no FR id, so `capabilities().shipped` cannot announce them.
- What a declaration offers may grow without its text changing. An act that sets a status board's field to a value of its own (`book` setting `status` to `"booked"`) is a move to that value's column (FR-108), where a board offered only a free `set-<field>` act; where a named step reaches a column, the free act no longer does. A TypeScript mutation says the constants it sets as `sets`, optional, and one without it reads as before.
- Who the people are arrived the same way, with no FR id (the Graview Roadmap's f-people-kind, f-act-as-me, f-own-end-grants and "visibility scoped by relation"), each optional: `kinds.<kind>.people` (`true` on one kind: a record of it whose id is a principal's id is that person; the declaration's `people: true`, which the installation's `user` says), `policy.grants[].ownEnd` (`true`: every record the call names at the far end of the link the act connects or severs is the principal's own, and every link the act would make or break has the principal's own record at one end — so a connect on a relation of one that would replace somebody else's link is refused; a seat with no id of its own is never offered one) and `policy.sees[].via` (a relation: a record of the sight's kinds is seen only where that relation joins it, at either end, to the principal's own record; `own` reads every relation and what they made). `$me` in an act's effect is the acting person's own record of the people kind — the person, for an agent acting for one — and never an argument, so a document that used `$me` as an argument's name now means the acting person by it; an act that reaches `$me` for a principal with no such record is refused as `refused`, with a sentence. An op whose act wrote its author's own record where its call never named it — `$me`, or `ctx.me` in TypeScript — is undone only by that person (or their agent, or the system): anybody else is refused with a sentence, since the same call by them would have done something else. A document edit's `rename-relation` carries a sight's `via` with it, and `remove-relation` is refused while a sight reads the relation, as it is while a lens draws by it. A TypeScript act reads the same id as `ctx.me`. The checker's codes for them are `people-ambiguous`, `people-unsaid`, `sight-via-unknown-edge`, `sight-via-misses-people`, `grant-own-end-without-link` and a document's `act-me`; none fires on a declaration that says none of the new keys and no `$me`. A kind's JSON Schema says `"x-graview-people": true` on the people kind.
- The edit vocabulary gained the people and the policy (FR-170): `set-people` (`{ kind, people }`; `true` is refused as `people-ambiguous` while another kind is the people, so a move is `false` on the one, then `true` on the other), `add-grant` and `add-sight` (a grant or a sight as `policy.grants[]` and `policy.sees[]` hold one; a role the document's `roles` does not list joins it; a first sight on a document with no policy comes with a grant to everyone of every act, since a sight alone would take every act away), and `remove-grant` and `remove-sight` (named by what they say: a grant's `roles` and `mutations`, a sight's `roles` and `kinds`, each list in any order, and any other key given must match too; two that match are refused, asking for the key that tells them apart; a grant on no kind, `kinds: []`, gives nothing and is refused). `remove-kind` takes the kind's derived `edit-<kind>` and `remove-<kind>` out of every grant, and a grant left with no act or no kind goes; it is refused while every sight shows only that kind, since the sights gone would show everyone everything, so a change says `remove-sight` first. What the change leaves the people and the policy saying together is judged once it is whole, and refused at its last such edit by the checker's own codes (`people-unsaid`, `sight-via-unknown-edge`, `sight-via-misses-people`, `grant-own-end-without-link`); `grant-act` and `sight-kind` name an act or a kind the document lacks. `DocumentDiff`'s sentences say a grant, a sight, a role and the people kind in the words the edits say them, where a policy changed was "Who may do what changes." (still said of a change those do not cover). The studio says a grant, a sight and the people kind it changed as these ops, where a grant or a sight was a `studio-unsaid` finding and the people kind was not said at all. A build that predates them refuses the ops as an edit it does not know, so a host reads `capabilities().shipped` for FR-170 before it offers them.
- The rule language gained archived records (FR-173), optional within `graview-document@1`: `all('<kind>')` reads the live records as before, `all('<kind>', true)` the archived ones and `all('<kind>', 'all')` both, and `archived()` (or `archived(<record>)`) says whether a record is archived. An archived record is out of every computed field, fact, rule and count that does not ask for it, so a rule over a graph with none archived judges as before. A grant, a rule's repair and `editDocument`'s rename and removal of a kind read `archive-<kind>`, `unarchive-<kind>` and `merge-<kind>` as they read `edit-<kind>` and `remove-<kind>`, and `graview check` knows them, so a grant naming one is no longer `grant-unknown-mutation`.
- A kind that is never archived arrived the same way (FR-173): `kinds.<kind>.archives`, only ever `false`, says what `defineNode({ archives: false })` says — the kind is given its `edit-` and `remove-<kind>` and no `archive-`, `unarchive-` or `merge-<kind>` — and `toDocument` writes it. A document without it archives every kind as before. A grant naming one of the three on such a kind is `grant-act`, as a grant naming any act the app lacks is. The edit vocabulary gained `set-archives` (`{ kind, archives }`), which says what the app stops or starts offering and is refused as `grant-unknown-mutation` while a grant names one of the three. `planMigration` brings back, in the same op and said, a record already archived of a kind the change makes never archived (`counts.broughtBack`), and keeps `$archived` on every other record it plans, where it used to clear it.
- The app's locale says more than its money (FR-178), with no new key: `brand.locale` (a document's and a declaration's) is what every day, time and number is said in on every face, through `Intl` — a record's facts and glance, a template's `{due}` and `{due | date}`, a moment's `{at}`, a block's field, a rule's line, the calendar, the timeline's hours, the seat's lines, an arrangement's headings — and it is en-US where it names none: "Sep 10, 2023", "3:30 PM", "1,250", where every day was said day first before ("10 Sep 2023"). A host passes the reader's locale as `locale` on the embed, `GraviewProvider` and a pages `PageContext`, which wins over the brand's. What changes is the order and the punctuation of the words a person reads, never a stored value, an op, a tool schema or a finding code; `editDocument`'s and `diffDocuments`' sentences about a locale say "Days, times, numbers and money are written for …", and `describeApp` says what the locale makes of a day, a time and a figure. A host that matched the old day-first words reads them from its build's `capabilities().shipped`, FR-178.
- What a list offers to filter by arrived the same way, with no FR id (0.1.29, the Roadmap's f-filters-that-scale): `pages.lists`, `{ "<kind>": { "filters": [...] } }`, names in order what a kind's list offers — a field, a relation, `is`, or `<relation>.<field>` (a choice at the far end of a relation); a list a document does not name offers what it offered before. `arrange-pages` takes `filters: { "<kind>": [...] | null }` and refuses a key the kind cannot be filtered by, and a filter's grammar takes `<relation>.<field>:<value>`. A template's formatter `excerpt` (`{summary|excerpt}`, `{summary|excerpt: <20–1000>}`) arrived with it, the same way: a build that predates it refuses the template. The finding codes that came with them are warnings and judge only what is new: `pages-filter-unknown` (a filter the kind cannot be filtered by, passed over), `pages-kind-unknown`, the code it was, which now also says a kind `pages.lists` names that is not there and `view-whole-text` (a card or a row that puts a `text` field whole in a text block, which is clamped).
- The order and groups a kind's list opens in arrived the same way, with no FR id (0.1.30, asked while prioritizing the Graview Roadmap): `pages.lists.<kind>.sort` (`"<key>"` or `{ "by", "direction"?, "then"? }`, a field, a computed field or `label`) and `pages.lists.<kind>.group` (`"<field>"` or `{ "by", "order"?, "closed"? }`, a choice or yes-or-no field), beside `filters`; a list a document does not order or group opens as it did before. `arrange-pages` takes `sort: { "<kind>": … | null }` and `group: { "<kind>": … | null }`, which a build that predates them refuses as keys it does not know. Unlike `pages-filter-unknown`, the finding that came with them, `pages-list-arrangement`, is an error: a list sorted by what the kind does not have, grouped by a field that is not a choice or a yes or no, or ordering or closing a value that is not one of its choices is refused, since such a list would open some other way unsaid; only a document that says the new keys can meet it.
- How a number is said arrived with no new key (0.1.29, the money bug found on a Cloud app): a number field's `format` (`money`, `percent`) and `unit`, which a document always held, are now said on every face, and a number's `"format": "duration"` now means exactly the `duration` type — whole minutes, said, typed and described to a tool as that type is (`x-graview-type: "duration"`), its `unit` no longer read. The edit vocabulary gained `set-format` (`{ kind, field, format?, unit? }`, `null` clearing either): a number's `money`, `percent` or `duration` and `unit`, or a text field's `markdown` (FR-180), refused on a field the format does not fit, which a build that predates it refuses as an edit it does not know. `add-field` and `retype-field` refuse a format on a field it does not fit, which they took silently before for a number's format. One checker code, `field-format`, says a format on a field it does not fit in one sentence ("`"format": "money"` is a number's format, and this field is a text"): an error for `markdown`, a warning for a number's format, which a declaration could always hold; and a note for a number shown as a duration, which the type says once. `money-currency` warns of money with neither `brand.currency` nor a currency `unit`.
- No key is taken away from a document format within its version, and none is renamed without the old name still being read. 0.1.16 broke this: its American spelling pass renamed a setting's `honored` (was `honoured`) in the document as well as in the declaration, and its notes said the document format was unchanged, so every document `toDocument` wrote before 0.1.16 that carried settings failed to compile ("Nothing knows how to apply undefined"). Since 0.1.17 (FR-134), a key renamed within a format is a line in `RESPELLED` (`@graview/core/document`): every reader — `readDocument`, `compileDocument`, `appFrom` and `appFromOrCompile` on a compiled app an older build made, `diffDocuments` and `editDocument` — reads the old name as the new one, keeps the new one when a document says both, and never changes the document handed; `toDocument` and an edit write the new name. `respellDocument` does the same for a host and says which paths it respelled. A document stored with the old name is read the same on every later build of the major, so a host need not rewrite it, though its next save writes the new name. `packages/core/tests/document/fixtures/` keeps documents and compiled apps as older builds wrote them, made by those builds from npm, and each must compile; a test records every key path a document has been able to carry and fails when one is no longer read, by either name.
- What the app's own actor may tidy on its own (0.1.30) arrived the same way: `kinds.<kind>.tidying` (`"never"` or `"no-links"`) and `kinds.<kind>.edges.<relation>.tidying` (`"never"`), optional in `graview-document@1`, and the edit `set-tidying` (`{ kind, relation?, tidying: "never" | "no-links" | "allowed" }`), said in a sentence by `editDocument` and the same sentence by `diffDocuments`. A kind that says `"never"` is given no `leave-alone-<kind>` or `allow-tidying-<kind>`, and a grant naming one is the error `grant-act`; a relation that says what its kind already says is the warning `tidying-redundant`. A build that predates them refuses the keys as `unknown-key`.
- One design proposed from a declaration arrived with no new key (Roadmap f-design-composer): `composeDesign(document | app, { records? })` and `inferJobs(document | app, { records? })` on `@graview/core/compose`. What they propose is a judgment a version may change — another job, another edit, another color of `ACCENT_PALETTE` — and that is not a break. What is kept: `composeDesign` answers `{ edits, said }`, every edit one `editDocument` of the same version accepts in turn, applied in one change to a document that compiled giving one that compiles with no warning from `designFindings`; `inferJobs` answers at most `MOST_INFERRED_JOBS` jobs, each one `graview check` accepts; and neither draws anything or changes a document by itself. The critic's `design-job-unanswered` changed meaning with the derived home that answers jobs: it is said only of a declared home that lists none of a job's kind, with nothing titled over it, and it now carries the `set-home` that answers it.
- What a declaration is made of arrived with no new key (Roadmap f-document-traits): `traitsOf(document | app)` on `@graview/core/compose` answers the traits a declaration carries, each one of the closed vocabulary `TRAITS` — `owners`, `status`, `schedule`, `budget`, `places`, `sources`, `stock`, `votes`, `private`, `history`, `publishing`, `roster`, `routines`, `comparison` — with the kinds, fields (`<kind>.<field>`), relations (`<kind>.<relation>`), rules, lenses (by title) and acts that carry it, its words (`TRAIT_WORDS`) and one sentence. The vocabulary is the surface: a name in `TRAITS` is never renamed or taken away within the major, and one added is said in the changelog, so a host that keeps a person's answers by trait name reads them on every later build. Which traits a given declaration is read to carry, and the sentence each is said in, are a judgment a version may sharpen — read only where the declaration leaves no doubt, as `inferJobs` is — and that is not a break; what is kept is that every carrier named is in the document and that nothing is read off prose.
- A starting document composed from parts arrived the same way (Roadmap f-compose-from-parts): `startingDocument({ base?, drop?, add?, name, purpose? })` on `@graview/core/compose` answers `{ document, took, left, said }` — the base's document (or one kind from nothing) with each dropped kind taken out with what only it served, each dropped trait's own carriers taken out, and each added trait's module brought in joined to the kind people see most; `took` and `left` name each part (`{ part, what, from }`: a kind, field, relation, rule, lens, act, sight or trait, from the base's name or the trait that brought it). What is kept: every change is one `editDocument` of the same version accepts in turn, the document compiles with no warning, a trait the base already carries is left as it is, and a dropped kind takes only what served it alone. What each module is made of — the field names, the acts, the rule — is a judgment a version may change, and that is not a break. Two of `editDocument`'s edits do more than they did, with no new key: `remove-kind` now takes the kind's hue out of `brand.accents`, the sights `via` a relation that went with the kind, and, when the kind was the people, the acts on the acting person's own record (`$me`), where it left each behind for the checker to refuse; `rename-kind` moves the hue with the kind.
- A Notion database as a connection arrived the same way (Roadmap f-notion-connection): `connections.<name>` may say `"system": "notion"` with `database` (its 32-character id, or `{ "env" }`), `kind`, optional `properties` (field → property name, or `{ "name", "type" }`), `auth`, `direction`, `conflicts`, `every` and `paused`; a `"google-calendar"` connection is read as before. The checker judges it with the codes a calendar's are judged with (`connection-kind`, `connection-field`, `connection-field-type`, `connection-creates`, `connection-edit`, `connection-remove`) and three new ones: the error `connection-properties` (a connection that would keep nothing in step), the warning `connection-read-only` (a people property, which is only read), and the error `connection-secret`, which refuses an integration's secret written anywhere in a connection — the one new error a declaration that passed before could meet, and only by holding a secret. A build that predates it refuses `"system": "notion"` by path, so a host writes one only on a build that has it. What a connection keeps between runs is the `SyncState` it always was; a Notion connection's `cursor` is its own JSON (the last `last_edited_time` it saw and when it last read the whole database), which a host keeps without reading. A Notion connection's relations kept as edges (Roadmap f-notion-several-tables) are additive too: a key of `properties` may name one of the kind's edges, mapped to a relation property (a property's `type` may be `"relation"`), and the checker gains the errors `connection-relation` (a relation property mapped to a field, or another type to an edge), `connection-relation-target` (an edge to a kind no Notion connection of the app keeps) and `connection-connect` (no act a link lands through), and the warning `connection-disconnect` — none of them met by a declaration that maps no edge. A `SyncState` may carry `unresolved`, the pages a relation reaches that no connection has linked yet, still format 1: a build that predates it drops it.
- A finding may carry `details` and `fixes` (Roadmap f-connection-refusal-in-plain-words, FR-229), beside `message`, `fix` and `edits`, which mean what they meant: `details` is the framework's own sentence where `message` is the person's, and `fixes` is the ways out a host offers as buttons, each `{ label, edits? }` with its edits in `editDocument`'s words where one can be written. `connection-creates` is the first to say them: where a calendar or a Notion connection names a kind no act makes from the event's or the page's fields alone, its `message` is "Blocks need a Type, and Google events don't have one." and its `fix` the three ways in one sentence, where it was the framework's sentence naming the act and the arguments, which is now its `details`; its code and its path are what they were. The edit vocabulary gained `set-connection` (`{ name, connection }` sets or replaces `connections.<name>` whole, judged for its shape there and for its kind, fields and acts by the checker; `connection: null` takes it away), which a build that predates it refuses as an edit it does not know, so a host reads `capabilities().shipped` for FR-229 before it offers a fix that carries one. `checkApp`'s findings carry the same two keys, and `graview check` prints them beneath the sentence (`details:`, then `fix: <label>` with each edit).
- A weekly record is one recurring event (Roadmap f-connection-weekly-records-recur, FR-230), with one new key: a Google calendar connection's `fields` may name `days`, a field that is an enum of weekdays or a list holding `mon` to `sun`; then `start` and `end` name string fields holding times of day (`"09:00"`), and each record is one event with a weekly rule in the app's `brand.timeZone`, its first week the week it is first sent. A `start` that repeats (`"repeats": true`) needs no new key: its repeat is the event's RRULE and each day set apart an EXDATE, and a recurring event made in the calendar is a record with its repeat, made and then given it through `edit-<kind>` in one batch. A build that predates it refuses `days` by path (`connections.<name>.fields`), and judged a repeating start as a one-off event. `connection-field-type` judges the new shapes at their paths (a `days` field that is not weekdays; a start or end that is not words beside `days`); no declaration that passed is refused. `SyncState` is what it was; what a connection's engine is handed to make a record (`createInbound`) may now say `then`, the acts that follow the making act in its batch.
- Formulas join text and build a date-time, and an act carries a change across a link (Roadmap f-formula-text-datetime, f-acts-update-linked). The rule language gained `concat`, `format`, `datetime` (and its alias `at`), `addMinutes`, `weekday` and `startOfWeek`; an expression that parsed before means what it meant, and a build that predates them refuses each as `unknown-function`. `format`'s pattern is a closed vocabulary (`EEE`, `EEEE`, `d`, `MMM`, `MMMM`, `yyyy`, `h:mm a`, `HH:mm`, words in single quotes), said in the app's `brand.locale` and on its `brand.timeZone` — never the reader's — and a moment built lands as a datetime field keeps one (an instant in UTC); an app that says no zone builds on UTC. `graview check` judges what the declaration alone shows as `expr-type` and `format-pattern` at the expression's path; `compileDocumentWithoutCheck` and a page say nothing new. An act gained `setsLinked` (`{ "<relation>": { "<field>": value } }`, on an act with `on`), optional, an act without it doing what it did; a build that predates it refuses the key by path. `effectsOf` may return a `LinkedSetEffect` (`{ set, through }`) beside the effects a document lists, a mutation definition may say `writesLinked`, and `graview-compiled@1` carries the new effect in an act's plan: a page that predates it would not run that effect, so a host serves a compiled app from the build that compiled it, as it does. The store refuses such an act, naming the record, where the principal may not run the far kind's own edit on one of the records reached; the derived tools and their input schemas are unchanged. The far kind's own edit still offers a carried field.

#### 5. Derived tool names and input schemas

Tools are derived from the declaration (`createToolRuntime`, `graview mcp`), and a model that listed them before a change sends what it learned then.

- A change to a derived tool's name, description or input schema for an unchanged declaration is called out in a `Compatibility:` line, even when it is a fix.
- A change caused by the declaration (a renamed field renames an argument) is the app's change, not the framework's. The framework's part is saying which tools moved.
- FR-110 is such a change. Every derived `edit-<kind>` says `additionalProperties: false`, so an argument it does not take is refused as `invalid` where it was dropped. A document's act always says its `writes`, read off what its `sets` and effects set on its subject (`[]` when that is nothing), so an argument that only feeds a record the act makes no longer counts as a write of the subject, and `edit-<kind>` offers that field again. The conformance kit announces the two fixtures it moved (`document:vendors`, `document:two-lines`, 0.1.14). A TypeScript mutation that declares no `writes` is read as before.
- FR-121 is such a change. Every act's tool says `additionalProperties: false` — a document's act, a TypeScript mutation whose input is a plain `z.object`, `remove-<kind>` — and a call with an argument the act does not take is refused as `invalid`, naming what it takes, where the argument was dropped and the act ran without it. An act that creates still takes `id`. An input its author made `z.looseObject`, or gave a `catchall`, keeps what it is not told about and its tool says nothing new; one that is not an object's shape is not judged. An argument given as `undefined` is no argument. The conformance kit announces the two fixtures it moved (`document:vendors`, `document:two-lines`, 0.1.15).

- A file field's argument (FR-162) is described as an object of `href`, `name`, `type` and `bytes`, with `width`, `height` and `caption` optional, and a list of them as an array of that object; a seat may set one to a value the host's upload gave, and a value whose `href` is not a path on the host is refused as `invalid`. The derived `edit-<kind>` of a declaration that has no such field is unchanged.

- A number field's argument with a `format` or a `unit` (0.1.29) is described with `"x-graview-format"` (`money`, `percent`, `duration`, or `unit` for a measure), `"x-graview-currency"` for money and `"x-graview-unit"` for a measure or a duration, and a description saying the value is a plain number ("An amount of money in USD: a plain number, 1250.5 for 1,250.50 USD."; "A fraction said as a percent: 0.15 is 15%."), after the field's own description where it has one; the type and range are unchanged. The conformance kit announces it on `document:vendors`.

- An app-link field's argument (FR-171) is described as a string of at most 500 characters with the address's `pattern` and `"x-graview-app-link": true`; a seat sets it to another app's address, and anything else is refused as `invalid`. The derived `edit-<kind>` of a declaration that has no such field is unchanged.

- A relation to another app's kind (FR-171) is an argument of the derived `edit-<kind>`, described as a string of at most 300 characters — or an array of at most 200 — with `"x-graview-linked": { address, kinds, cardinality }` and a description saying it is `"<kind>:<id>"`; a seat finds the value with `find_linked` (`relation`, `query`, `of`, `limit`), a read listed only for an app with such a relation, answered through the host's `linkedRecords` as the seat. The tools of an app with no such relation are unchanged.

- A Markdown field's argument (FR-180) is described as the text field's string with `"contentMediaType": "text/markdown"` and its description ending "Written in Markdown."; what it takes is unchanged. A derived edit's history line says a string longer than 60 characters by its start (`excerpt`), not whole.

- A phone, a place and a duration field's argument says which with `"x-graview-type": "phone" | "place" | "duration"`, and a duration's `"x-graview-unit": "minutes"`; a field that says nothing of itself is described in words ("A length of time in whole minutes: 90 is 1 h 30 min."). A phone is a string with the phone's `pattern`, a place a string, a duration an `integer` of at least 0: a seat sends 90, never "1h 30m", which is refused as `invalid`. The derived `edit-<kind>` of a declaration that has none of these fields is unchanged.

- A date that repeats is described to a seat as an object of `every`, `interval`, `on`, `until`, `count`, `except` and `continues`, `additionalProperties: false`, with `"x-graview-repeat": true`, or `null`; the derived `edit-<kind>` of a kind with one takes it beside the date. Such a kind gains three derived acts, permitted as its edit is: `skip-<kind>` ("Skip this one", `{ id, on }`), `detach-<kind>` ("Change just this one", `{ id, on, …fields }`: a record of its own on that day, with the series' fields and the links the series makes, and the day an exception on the series) and `split-<kind>` ("Change from here", `{ id, on, …fields }`: the series ends the day before and a new one, `continues` naming it, starts that day); `field` names the date where a kind has more than one that repeats. Each refuses a day the series does not fall on as `refused`. A kind with no date that repeats gains none, and its tools are unchanged.

- Drawing a view and keeping it as a lens arrived as two tools a host opts into (the seat as a guide, B3): `draft_view`, a read, and `keep_lens`, which hands the host's `drafts.keep` the `add-lens` edit. A runtime lists them only when given `drafts` (`keep_lens` only with `drafts.keep`, and never on a read-only seat), and `toolDefinitions` only when told `drafts: "draw"` or `"keep"`, so a surface that did not ask keeps its tools and its hash. Their names, input schemas and answers are held to this section from now on. A lens either tool takes or returns is a declared lens (`{ title, lens, on, bindings?, options? }`) and is judged as one under the seat's sight; a kind the seat may not see is answered as one that is not there.

- FR-167 moved the read tools' answers and three input schemas. Every read answers at most `READ_CHARS` (8,000) characters of JSON, for a seat's turn and an MCP client alike. `get_graph` takes `offset` and answers a page of at most 25 records, the edges out of them, `total` and, when there are more, `more`; `get_node` takes `offset` and answers its links as `{ kind, id, label }`, 20 each way a page, where it answered whole edges; `get_violations` takes `offset` and answers `{ violations, total, more? }` where it answered an array; `search_graph` answers at most 20 hits whatever `limit` asked, with `more` and without `matched`. A field's text past 600 characters is cut and says its length, and any other read too long to fit answers `{ cut, partial }`. Within a host's turn, a call repeated with the same input is answered `{ already }`.

- FR-173 added three derived acts to every kind, beside `edit-<kind>` and `remove-<kind>`: `archive-<kind>` and `unarchive-<kind>` (`{ id }`, "Bring it back") and `merge-<kind>` (`{ id, into }`: the record `id` is archived and `into` takes its links). None is destructive; each is permitted through the acts that create the kind, as `remove-<kind>` is, and a grant may name each on its own. An app that declares an act of one of these names keeps its own. `search_graph` and `get_graph` take `archived` — `false` when unsaid, `true`, or `"all"` — and reach only the live records unless it is given; `get_node` reads an archived record by its id and says `archived: true`, as its links to one do.
