- Whether the roles you chose generalize, or merely rename your own fields.

---

Build a Graview lens that binds ROLES rather than field names, so a second domain can reuse it unchanged — and prove the reuse rather than asserting it.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-lens.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-linked-records.html

# graview-linked-records

`graview-linked-records` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Link a record in one Graview app to a record in another app — a relation whose target is another app's kind, read there as whoever is looking, walked by computed fields and rules, its far changes kept in this app's history — and verify it with graview check and by opening it as a viewer who may not see the other app.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Link a record in another app

A relation usually goes to a kind of the same app. When the thing lives in an app of its own — a purchase scenario that buys a house kept in the house app — the relation goes THERE: its target is `@` + the other app's address + `/` + its kind. Linking picks a record in that app; the other app is never changed. What the far record is, and whether this viewer may see it, is the host's to say, every time, as the viewer.

### Do this

1. **Declare the relation to the other app's kind.** In a document:

```json "scenario": { "fields": { "name": { "type": "string", "required": true }, "budget": { "type": "number", "format": "money" } }, "edges": { "forHouse": { "to": ["@nick/house/house"], "cardinality": "one", "description": "the house this scenario buys" } } } ```

The address is the one an `app-link` field would hold: `@owner/app`, the id the host knows the app by (`@app_kf5eydr9z58jzf/house`), or its https address (`@https://example.com/a/house/house`). Every target names ONE app; mix in a kind of this app, a second app, an `inverse` or `appendOnly`, and the check refuses it in a sentence. In TypeScript the link is a field it is kept in: `forHouse: linkedRecordField("@nick/house/house").optional()` (`{ cardinality: "many" }` for several). A host that changes a document by edits sends `{"op": "add-relation", "kind": "scenario", "relation": "forHouse", "to": ["@nick/house/house"], "cardinality": "one"}`, refused by the same finding codes; the studio makes one with its act for linking another app's records.

1. **Let the record's own edit link one.** The link is kept on the record that links, as the far kind and its id — `"house:h1"`, or a list — so the derived `edit-scenario` sets it, undoes it, logs it and hides it from a seat a sight keeps it from, like any field. The faces draw a picker that lists what the host finds there for this viewer; an agent finds the value with `find_linked` and passes it to the edit. A declared act may not `connects` it or set it (`act-linked`).

1. **Walk it by name.** `forHouse.listPrice` reads the far record's field, in a computed field, a view's block or a rule:

```json "computed": { "price": { "expr": "forHouse.listPrice", "label": "Asking price" } }, "rules": { "within-budget": { "over": "scenario", "when": "budget != null", "require": "forHouse.listPrice <= budget" } } ```

It is read AS THE VIEWER: a field they may not see there reads as nothing. A link they may not open, or not read yet, is said, never thrown — the computed value says why it has none, and a rule that would fail without it is "could not be judged" rather than broken. `out('forHouse')` does not walk it (`rule-linked`).

1. **Show it.** A record's page and the scene's record panel draw the far record with its own card — label, describe line, a glance at its fields, its app's name — and `{ "field": "forHouse" }` in a card names it. Pressing it opens it in its own app through the host. A viewer who may not open that app sees "linked record (no access)" and nothing of it.

1. **Hand the host's reader in.** The host implements `LinkedRecords` and passes it where it passes `resolveApp` (`mount`, `<Embed>`, `GraviewProvider`, `PagesApp`) as `linkedRecords`: `resolve(ref, viewer)` answers `{ address, kind, id, label, describe?, card?, fields, href?, app? }`, `{ denied: true }` or `null`; `find({ address, kinds, query, limit }, viewer)` the records it may link; `open(ref, viewer)`, optional, opens one in place. `linkedRecordsOver({ "@nick/house": { store, name, opens, href } })` from `@graview/core/linked` is that host over stores in memory — tests and a host holding both apps use it as is. When the far record changes there, the host calls `recordLinkedChange(store, { ref, fields, app })`: one op per linking record, authored by the far app, naming what changed and none of its values, so Activity and the record's history say it.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build && npx graview check ./app.gdd.json
npx graview describe ./app.gdd.json   # "Linked from other apps" says each relation and how to link one
```

Report **the actual output**. What it catches here: `linked-target`, `linked-mixed`, `linked-apps`, `linked-inverse`, `linked-append-only`, `act-linked`, `rule-linked`. Then open a record that links one as a viewer the host refuses that app, and confirm the page says "linked record (no access)" and shows nothing of it — not its name, not a value worked out from it.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether the other app exists, has that kind, or lets this viewer in: the host answers that, every time, and nothing in the document can.
- Whether a far field the expression names (`listPrice`) is one the other app has: a field it lacks, or hides from this viewer, reads as nothing.
- Whether linking across apps was the right shape at all. If both kinds change together and the same people keep them, one app with a local relation is simpler.

---

Link a record in one Graview app to a record in another app — a relation whose target is another app's kind, read there as whoever is looking, walked by computed fields and rules, its far changes kept in this app's history — and verify it with graview check and by opening it as a viewer who may not see the other app.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-linked-records.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-lists.html

# graview-lists

`graview-lists` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Keep a Graview app's lists usable as it grows — what a list offers to filter by, the order and groups it opens in, cards read at a glance, several records acted on at once, a list printed as a static page or exported as CSV, and a date that repeats rather than a record each time — and verify each with graview check and the page itself rather than assuming it.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Lists that stay usable as an app grows

A list that worked at twelve records stops working at three hundred: Filter lists every record at the far end of every relation, each card prints a thirty-line summary, and a weekly practice is fifty records. None of this needs a custom page: the declaration says what the list offers and the order it opens in, the templates how much of a long text a card shows, and a date repeats. Setting records aside, merging a duplicate and the app's own actor tidying are `graview-tidying`.

### Do this

1. **Say what a kind's list filters by.** In a document:

```json "pages": { "lists": { "request": { "filters": ["status", "area", "became", "became.stage"] } } } ```

In TypeScript, the same under `defineApp({ pages: { lists: … } })`. Each key is a field, a relation, `is`, or `<relation>.<field>` — a choice on the record at the far end ("The feature it became · Stage: Building"). The choice fields among them stand over the list as chips with counts; the rest are under Filter, each heading closed until pressed, with a box that finds a filter or a far record by a few letters. Unsaid, a list offers every way but a relation to a kind with more than forty records (offered by that kind's choices instead), and its first two choice fields as chips. An address says the same: `/requests?filter=status:open`.

**Say the order and grouping it opens in**, beside its filters:

```json "feature": { "sort": { "by": "rank", "direction": "desc", "then": "name" } }, "request": { "group": { "by": "status", "order": ["planned", "new"], "closed": ["done", "declined"] } } ```

`sort` is a field, a computed field (a rank the kind works out) or `label`, lowest first unless `"desc"`, with a `then` for ties; `group` is a choice or yes-or-no field (`"true"`, `"false"`). `order` puts its groups first; `closed` ones are drawn last and shut, each a button saying "done · 12 requests" that opens it (`?open=done` keeps it open; words in the Find box open them all). A person still sorts or groups the list another way from its arranging line. The edit is `arrange-pages` with `sort: { "<kind>": … | null }` and `group: { "<kind>": … | null }`.

1. **Let a card say a long text's start.** A card shows a `text` field in three lines at most and a row in one, cut with an ellipsis. Say it on purpose with the `excerpt` formatter — `{summary|excerpt}` is its first sentence or about 140 characters cut at a word, `{summary|excerpt: 80}` at most 80 (20 to 1000) — and leave the whole text to the record's page. A list block draws 100, then "Show 58 more" (`limit` up to 1000); `group: "inGenre"` heads it by linked record. Markdown prose says so — `{"type": "text", "format": "markdown"}`, or `markdownField()` — and the record's page draws it as prose (headings, lists, links, code; no HTML), while a row, a card, a describe line and a search hit say its first paragraph or about 160 characters with the syntax taken out. A card with no blocks of its own says its kind's `glance` — exactly those fields, nothing after them; prose there is a line under the chips, never a cut chip. A choice another chip beside it shares (a severity and a confidence, both "high") says its field: "Confidence: high". A related record in a template is said by its kind's `label`: `{out('affects') | and}` is "src/files.ts and tsconfig.json"; a count starting a headline, `{n | words | capital}`, is "Two findings". A place titled as a kind's list is keeps the name on the bar, and the list folds into More as "All root causes" (`pages-place-named-as-a-list`).

1. **Print a place when a fixed link wants one.** `renderPlace(store, app, "/requests", { viewer, locale })` from `@graview/pages/static` answers `{ html, css, title, found }`: one self-contained page, no script, in the app's look, under the viewer's sight, the same words the routed face says. It imports no React, so a Worker renders it on each change. A `design` puts it in the product's own markup — `records[kind](record, site)` writes a record's page, `document(page)` what goes around it — which is how graview.dev renders its pages (`apps/site/design.mjs`).

1. **Know what a kind opens to before you draw it a picture.** Gone into with no lens of its own (`#focus=aggregate:room`), a kind opens to its stop: its plural, count and description; its creating act first ("Add a room"), asked in place; how many are overdue or due this week on its due date; its problems counted by rule, each opening its repairs; what changed since this reader last looked; and a picture its data chooses — a board by its main choice (`status`, `stage`, `state`, `phase` or the lifecycle's field) up to 300 records, a calendar where today's month has short records on its main date, else a table of its glance and its relations, 50 rows at a time. "Keep as a lens" declares that picture (`add-lens`). So give a kind a lifecycle or a `status`, a `glance`, and a creating act with a `title` before you write it a view.

1. **Let several be done at once — it is already there.** A kind's list, a kind's stop and a board choose records: a box at each row's start on a desk, Shift for a range, Cmd/Ctrl-A, Escape; the boxes one Tab stop, the arrows between them, Space to choose; a long press on a phone. The bar offers the acts every chosen record shares (`actsForSeveral` in `@graview/tools/several`): acts on the subject alone ("Mark it done") and those that ask once for all ("Move the date…"), "Move to <value>" for the kind's state field, archive, merge and remove behind More. One press is `actOnSeveral`: one batch, one undo. A record the act may not run on (the policy, the seat's sight, the act's own refusal) is named and stays chosen; the rest apply. A seat does the same with `act_on_several` (`{ act, records, args }`). So declare acts on a `subject` with as few other arguments as they need.

1. **Let a weekly practice be one record, not fifty.** A date that repeats is `{ "type": "date", "repeats": true }` (or `"datetime"`) in a document, `startsAtRepeat: repeatField()` beside `startsAt` in TypeScript. The record keeps its first occurrence in the date and the rule beside it: `"startsAtRepeat": { "every": "week", "on": ["tue"], "until": "2026-12-15" }` (`every` day, week, month or year; `interval`; `on` weekdays or days of the month, `-1` the last; `until`; `count`; `except`). Nothing is stored per occurrence: a rule, a sort, `today()` and "due in the next 7 days" read the next one, a calendar draws each, marked, and a row says "Every Tuesday, next Oct 27". `skip-<kind>`, `detach-<kind>` ("Change just this one") and `split-<kind>` ("Change from here") take `{ id, on }`; the record's page changes the rule with a picker beside the date.

1. **Let a list leave as a spreadsheet — or say where it may not.** A kind's list and a lens that lists records (calendar, timeline, coverage, board, status board) offer "Export CSV" beside the heading or on the lens's arranging line, and in the place menu: the rows shown, in their order, filter, words and groups (a "Group" column first), the name, then each field as the page says it, under the seat's sight. Off for everyone with `"export": false` on the lens or under `pages.lists.<kind>`; the owner's menu says "Turn off export" (the edit `{ "op": "set-lens-export" }`). A host that saves files passes `onExport`.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
graview check src/domain/app.ts
```

It warns of a filter the kind cannot be filtered by (`pages-filter-unknown`) and names the keys it can, a kind `pages.lists` names that is not there (`pages-kind-unknown`); it refuses a list sorted by what the kind does not have, grouped by a field that is not a choice or a yes or no, or closing a value that is not one of its choices (`pages-list-arrangement`, an error, in a sentence); warns of an `export` that is not true or false (`lens-export-not-a-boolean`, `pages-list-export-not-a-boolean`) or on a lens with no records (`lens-export-lists-no-records`); and of a card or row that puts a `text` field whole in a text block (`view-whole-text`: "feature card shows summary whole; it will be clamped"). Then look at the list at a phone's width as well as a desk's:

```sh
graview describe src/domain/app.ts --place requests --seed seed.json --width 390
```

It says the list's headings, each record's card and what is filtered, as the page draws them. Run an act over three records, one of which it may not take: that one is named and stays chosen, and one undo takes back the rest.

A right-click on a row, a value or the page's ground opens the scene's menu on the pages (Shift+right-click, a text field or selected text keep the browser's). A design's own row takes part as a link to its record or with `data-graview-record`, its own value with `data-graview-field` and `data-graview-editable`, which adds "Change …" to the menu.

### What the check cannot see

Whether the filters you named are the ones a person reaches for — that is a question for someone who uses the list. Whether a card's first sentence is a useful one: `excerpt` cuts where the text does. And `renderPlace` writes no history and no acts by design; a host that wants them on paper writes them itself.

---

Keep a Graview app's lists usable as it grows — what a list offers to filter by, the order and groups it opens in, cards read at a glance, several records acted on at once, a list printed as a static page or exported as CSV, and a date that repeats rather than a record each time — and verify each with graview check and the page itself rather than assuming it.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-lists.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-locale.html

# graview-locale

`graview-locale` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Say a Graview app's money, days, times and numbers the way its people say them — a currency, a locale and a time zone declared once on the brand, a field kept as money, {net | money} and {at | time} in a template — and let graview check refuse a code, a locale or a zone it cannot write rather than trusting the page.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Money, days and times in the app's own words

A sum with no currency is a bare number, a date in somebody else's order is a misread deadline, and an instant said on the server's clock is a meeting missed by five hours. Each is said once, on the brand, and every face — record, list, card, table, form, rule and act sentence, Activity, the static page and a worker view — says it the same way. The rest of the brand, the name, mark, typeface and palette, is `graview-brand`.

### Do this

1. **Say its money.** `currency: "EUR"` and `locale: "de-DE"` on the brand (a document's `brand` may carry them alone, without an accent; the edit is `set-brand`) are what a sum is said in wherever a block names none: a figure or a field shown as money, and `{net | money}` in a template — "21.000 €". A block's own `currency` wins. Without one, sums are numbers.

1. **Mark a field as money.** A document field marked `"format": "money"` is said in it on every face — record, list, card, table, form ("$" beside the box, "$1,250.50" taken as typed) — and its own `"unit": "EUR"` wins. `set-format` changes only a field's format or unit.

1. **Say its days and numbers.** The locale says every day, time and number on every face: en-US unless it says ("Sep 10, 2023", "3:30 PM", "1,250"); "en-GB" keeps the day first. The reader's, a host's `locale` on the embed or the provider, wins over it.

1. **Say the clock an instant is read on.** `timeZone: "America/New_York"` (an IANA name, never an offset) is the clock every instant kept with a zone (`2026-10-16T14:47:00Z`) is said on: lists, record pages, an act's sentence and its echo to an agent, Activity, the date editor. A moment kept without a zone is still the wall time written. A person's zone wins where a host passes one — `timeZone` on `GraviewProvider`, the embed and the pages face, beside `locale`. A worker view is handed `locale` and `timeZone` rather than formatted strings (`graview-worker-view`).

1. **Say them in templates.** `{at | time}` ("10:47 AM"), `{at | datetime}` ("Oct 16, 2026, 10:47 AM EDT"), `{at | date}` and `relative` (an instant's day counted on the app's clock); a field block takes `as: "time"`, `as: "datetime"` and `as: "money"`.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build && npx graview check ./dist/domain/app.js
npx graview check --document app.json   # a document
```

It refuses what it cannot write — a currency that is not a three-letter code (`brand-currency`), a locale it does not know (`brand-locale`), a zone the runtime does not know or an offset (`brand-time-zone`) — and warns `money-currency` where a money field has neither its own unit nor the app's currency. Report what it said. Then open a record holding a sum and an instant with your machine's clock set elsewhere: the sum carries its symbol, and the time is on the declared clock, not the machine's.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether the zone is the one the people work in. A team across two zones wants each reader's zone passed by the host, not one declared for all.
- Whether a field that holds money was marked as money. An unmarked number is said as a number, faithfully.

---

Say a Graview app's money, days, times and numbers the way its people say them — a currency, a locale and a time zone declared once on the brand, a field kept as money, {net | money} and {at | time} in a template — and let graview check refuse a code, a locale or a zone it cannot write rather than trusting the page.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-locale.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-logo.html

# graview-logo

`graview-logo` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Put a client's own logo and page icon on a Graview app — inline SVG or a path, one for each scheme so a picture on white is not a white slab in the dark, an emoji as the icon — drawn in the default shell and handed to a design's own, and let graview check refuse a mark that could act rather than trusting it.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## A logo, and an icon

The brand's mark is drawn as it was given, never redrawn, on every face: the app bar, a design's shell, the static page, a worker view. The palette and the type are `graview-brand`; this is the picture beside the name.

### Do this

1. **One mark when it can be one.** Inline SVG with `currentColor` takes the accent and works in both schemes from one file:

```ts logo: '<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" ... stroke="currentColor">...</svg>', ```

1. **One for each scheme when it cannot.** A client's real logo — a JPG or PNG on white — sits as a white slab on a dark ground. Give the dark scheme its own:

```ts logo: { light: "/graview/assets/<sha>.jpg", dark: "/graview/assets/<sha>.png" }, ```

The light one is drawn in the light scheme, and in the dark too where there is no dark one. In a document the same object takes `alt`: `"logo": { "light": "…", "dark": "…", "alt": "TrueNorth Recon" }` (`{ "src", "alt" }` and a plain string still mean one logo).

1. **Inverting is asked for, never guessed.** Whether a light logo is a picture opaque on white cannot be known from it, so with no dark one nothing happens in the dark unless the brand says `darkFallback: "invert"`: then, in the dark scheme alone, it is drawn `invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg)` and screened onto the ground. Beside a `dark` one it is never used, and `graview check` says so (`brand-logo`).

1. **A design's shell draws it with `<AppMark brand={context.brand} />`** (`@graview/primitives`), as the default shell's bar does. Both marks are in the page, each `data-graview-scheme-only="light"` or `"dark"`, and the theme's sheet for the scheme the page is in hides the other's — so it switches with the scheme however the page chose it, with no hook. A design that draws its own `<img>` reads `logoFor(brand, scheme)` (`@graview/core`): `{ src, invert }`. Never a CSS filter of the design's own over the brand's logo.

1. **On Graview Cloud**, upload each with `add_image`, then `{"op": "set-brand", "logo": {"light": "/graview/assets/<sha>.jpg", "dark": "/graview/assets/<sha>.png"}}`. `set-brand` says what changed: "The logo gets one of its own for the dark scheme." `null` clears it.

### What a mark may be

- **Inline SVG or a path on the app's own host** in a document — never another origin. It is read element by element as the browser reads it: shapes, groups, gradients, filters, text and links to its own `#id`s, every attribute quoted, nothing after `</svg>`. A script, a handler, `<a>`, `<style>`, an animation, `foreignObject` or anything it loads is refused (`brand-mark`, at `brand.logo.light` or `brand.logo.dark`, with the reason), never rewritten. A declared app's mark may live at any address an image is drawn from; one that could act is refused the same.
- **The icon** (`favicon`) is a mark too, set only by a face that owns the page; an embed on somebody else's page leaves theirs alone unless the host passes `favicon: true`. `"favicon": { "emoji": "🏡" }` — exactly one standard emoji (👩🏽‍🌾 and 🇺🇸 count as one) — is the icon and, with no logo, the mark; anything else is refused (`brand-emoji`).

`describe_place("home")` says the app as the home draws it (its `masthead`): the name, the line under it, and the logo by its alt text.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build && npx graview check ./dist/domain/app.js
```

`brand-mark` and `brand-logo` say which mark, where and why. Then **look at it in both schemes** — `?theme=light` and `?theme=dark` — on the bar and in the design's own shell: the dark one in the dark, or the light one inverted only where the brand asked.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether the logo reads at 18 pixels. Most do not.
- Whether an inverted logo still looks like the client's: its hues stay, its lightness flips, so a navy mark comes out pale blue. If that matters, give a dark one.
- Whether the dark one is the client's at all. Ask for it.

---

Put a client's own logo and page icon on a Graview app — inline SVG or a path, one for each scheme so a picture on white is not a white slab in the dark, an emoji as the icon — drawn in the default shell and handed to a design's own, and let graview check refuse a mark that could act rather than trusting it.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-logo.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-new-app.html

# graview-new-app

`graview-new-app` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Start a product on Graview in its own repository — the shape of the declaration, the shell that comes for free, and the CI that keeps it honest afterwards.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Start a product on Graview

Graview ships as packages that share one version. A product built on it lives in **its own repository** and depends on them the way any other consumer does. This is the setup that gets you from nothing to something that can tell you when you have broken it.

### Start with the scaffolder

```sh
# from a framework checkout (the packages are not published yet):
pnpm install && pnpm build
pnpm graview create ../my-app --link . --name "My App" --kind thing
# once published, from anywhere:
npm create graview@latest my-app        # or: pnpm create graview my-app
```

Put the product BESIDE the framework, never inside its git tree; `--link` names it relative to where you run the command. `--workspace` writes the layout every real product ends up with (a root, the app under `app/`, the harnesses beside it); `--merge` starts in a repository that already has a README, naming collisions rather than writing over them.

It writes exactly the shape below — one kind with `creates`, `connects`, `writes` and a `lifecycle`, one rule with its repair, the shell, the routed face, a headless test, a CI workflow — installs it, installs these skills into it, and makes the first commit ("My App, on Graview"; staged instead when git has no identity). `AGENTS.md` at the root says the loop, the rules and the skills, and `CLAUDE.md` imports it; `verify` rewrites `docs/agents.md` and `docs/llms.txt`, which are committed. Run its `verify`, then replace the first kind with the product's own. The rest of this skill is what each part is for.

### The shape

```text
src/
  domain/            # No React in here. This is what `graview check` reads.
    schema.ts        # defineNode × n, createSchema (z comes from @graview/core)
    mutations.ts     # defineMutation × n — every change is a named, typed act
    invariants.ts    # defineInvariant × n — rules that name their repairs
    policy.ts        # who may do what, if anyone
    brand.ts         # name, mark, typeface, palette
    app.ts           # defineApp({ ... }) — one object, the whole surface
  ui/
    views.tsx        # registerDefaultViews, then your own where you care
    app.tsx          # the provider, the scene, the workbench
  main.tsx
```

`graview check` reads `defineApp`; a React import in `domain/` would drag a UI package into the checker.

**Or as one JSON document:** `app.json` (`"format": "graview-document"`, `$schema` `node_modules/@graview/core/dist/document.schema.json`, which types lenses and view blocks), then `graview check --document app.json`, `graview describe --document app.json`, `graview preview app.json --seed seed.json`. Kinds, acts and rules are kebab-case (`tool-note`), fields and relations camelCase (`supersededBy`). `preview --data` holds its folder: stop it to `sync-seed --apply`. In a framework checkout, `pnpm graview:link` puts `graview` on PATH.

### Do this

1. **Install.** The scaffold already did.

1. **Declare one kind, one mutation, one rule.** Not the whole domain. The loop you want on day one is: declare → `graview check` → look → declare more.

1. **Open it empty before you believe in it.** `graview describe ./dist/domain/app.js` reads out what a blank installation meets; `<Begin>` is that as a surface, wired into the scaffolded home. See `graview-seed`.

1. **Declare the seams that make the interface smart.** These are one-line declarations on mutations and kinds, and every derived surface reads them: - `creates: ["<kind>"]` on every mutation that adds a kind — the chain `Begin` and `graview describe` read, and the empty card's own way in. - `connects: [...]` / `severs: [...]` naming the edge kinds a mutation makes or breaks — what makes drawn LINES selectable, offers the act from either end, and hides a severing act with nothing to sever. - `lifecycle: { field, retired }` on kinds whose members expire — counts say "+N past". - `subject: { kinds, arg }` on every mutation that acts on a thing.

1. **Take the shell.** `Shell` from `@graview/primitives` is everything not about your domain: the one app bar an embed wears too (the name, the Scene and Pages switch, the scene's pictures, Find, Activity, the standing, the person), the scene, its key, the quick ask (⌘K, where the host gives a model) and the acts at the pointer. Its parts (`AppBar`, `Inspector`, `Standing`, `ActivityRail`, `Trail`, `OverviewButton`) are exported for a shell of your own; one is about eighty lines, and a longer one is probably rebuilding something derived. `firstLook` on `Shell` and `PagesApp` (`true` or `{ seen, onDone, steps }`) points a newcomer at the app's own controls once; write no tour.

Search comes with `Shell`: Find answers `/` or ⌘K from anywhere, lights what the words find in whatever picture is open and dims the rest, and `#q=` makes a search a stop Back returns to. Nothing is declared per kind.

The routed face is one branch in `main.tsx`: when the path starts with `/pages`, render `<PagesApp basename="/pages" context={{ store, brand, views: views(), settings }} />` from `@graview/pages`. It lands on a gallery of the app's pictures — every kind drawn as a card until you title a lens, then the lens by its name — with a list, a record and a form per kind, the problems and the map, at phone widths. Hand it the same `views` the scene draws from, or it has no pictures to land on.

1. **Register default views first, override later.** `registerDefaultViews` means a new kind renders sensibly at all three fidelities before you write anything. Write a custom view for a kind when the generic one is genuinely wrong, not on principle.

1. **Keep content in the graph.** What a page shows — a pitch's sections, a chart's tags — is records of a kind, seeded, never a JSON file a view imports: `graview check` names a face module that reads one (`face-reads-content-beside-the-graph`). A declaration change that loses nothing is made without asking; git keeps the way back.

1. **Add the check to your build.** `"check": "graview check ./dist/domain/app.js"`, and a `verify` that runs typecheck, test, build and check in that order. The scaffold writes both.

### What to make yours next

The scaffold is deliberately the framework's own face. A product replaces it in this order, and each step has a skill and a worked chapter in `apps/seedbed` behind it:

1. **Who it is for.** `purpose: { for, jobs }` on `defineApp` or the document: the questions its people bring, each a `kind`, a rule-language `where`, a `sort` and the next `act`. `graview check` holds each (`job-*`); describe and the seat read them (`@graview/core/jobs`).
2. **The words.** Every edge gets `description` and `inverse` — how it reads from each end — or `graview check` says `edge-without-inverse` and the far end is captioned with the edge kind's name. Every mutation gets a `title` and `description`; they are the button and the tool schema. (`graview-node-kind`.)
3. **A lens with a name.** A lens registered over a group with a `title` is a PLACE — a tab on the app bar, one press from anywhere. Start from the three that ship; write your own when the domain has a picture of itself, the way the garden has a map. (`graview-lens`, chapters 10-13.)
4. **The pages.** One page in the product's words first, then, when the product needs to look like a product, every surface: the shell, the home, the lists, the records, the problems — over the same store, acts, rules and permissions. (`graview-pages`, chapters 9 and 13.)
5. **A seat and a policy.** Who may do what, declared once; the strip, the pages and the agent's tools all narrow from it. (`graview-permissions`, `graview-agent-seat`, chapters 5 and 7.)
6. **A brand, and shipping.** The name, the mark, the typefaces, the palette the checker holds to AA; a version and a migration so a stored graph is carried forward. (`graview-brand`, `graview-ship`, chapters 8 and 12.)

Work with an agent beside the declaration: describe a kind, let it draft, run `pnpm verify`, look, declare more.

### The CI a product on Graview needs

Copy the shape from the framework's own `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, minus the packaging steps you do not need. What earns its place:

- **`tsc`** — an edge to an undeclared kind is a typecheck failure, so this catches a whole class before anything runs.
- **`graview check`** — everything `tsc` cannot see: a repair naming a mutation nobody registered, a lens role bound to a missing field, a role that may do nothing, a palette pair below AA. **Fail the build on errors.** Warnings are a judgment call; errors are not.
- **Headless tests** — the domain tier has no DOM in it. Test that your rules fire on graphs that break them and that their repairs resolve them; that is the test that catches a real regression.
- **An accessibility run, in BOTH schemes.** Copy `apps/todo/scripts/run-a11y.mjs`: the real accessibility tree through CDP, plus axe-core. A light palette that clears AA in the dark is what it catches.

### Supported browsers

Chromium, WebKit and Firefox, all verified (`pnpm engines`); the floor is `document.adoptedStyleSheets` (Safari 16.4+, Firefox 101+, Chromium 99+). The altitude morph rides `@property` and cuts cleanly where it is missing — write no fallback. `ai.onDevice` needs WebGPU or Chrome's Prompt API, else the seat says AI isn't available. The GPU is never a requirement.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm verify        # typecheck, tests, build, graview check
graview doctor     # one Graview release everywhere; React's pair; PATH from a checkout
```

Run the project's own `graview`, not `npx -y graview@<pin>`: inside a pnpm workspace holding the release, npx finds no bin.

Report the real output. On a new app the useful early findings are `mutation-untitled`, `mutation-undescribed`, `edge-without-inverse` and `required-invariant-unregistered` — things that look fine until somebody reads the interface or an agent reads a tool schema.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether your kinds are the right kinds. The test for each: does anything point AT it, and does it have a life of its own? A color is a field. A fixture is a kind.
- Whether your mutations are the acts a person would name. They are the labels in the strip and the instructions in an agent's tool schema, so an opaque one costs twice.
- Whether the interface is any good. Run it at the size it will have: seed a real catalog, not a dozen rows. The scene groups a relation too long for its band or closes it on "+N more", so a thousand records are a picture; whether the groups are the ones a person would ask for is yours to judge.

---

Start a product on Graview in its own repository — the shape of the declaration, the shell that comes for free, and the CI that keeps it honest afterwards.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-new-app.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-node-kind.html

# graview-node-kind

`graview-node-kind` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Add a node kind to a Graview app — fields, edges, label, plural and field roles — and verify it with graview check rather than claiming it worked.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Add a node kind

A kind is the unit of everything here. Declaring one gets you, without another line: a place in the layout, a card at three fidelities, an aggregate view, an accessibility label, a hue, and inclusion in every agent tool that walks the graph.

How its card, row and page read as data, and the values worked out from others that they show, is `graview-view-specs`.

### Do this

1. **Find the schema.** It is the file calling `createSchema`. Usually `src/domain/schema.ts`.

1. **Declare the kind.** Zod is the single source of runtime validation, TypeScript types and JSON Schema — there is no second place to describe a field.

```ts export const fixture = defineNode("fixture", { fields: z.object({ // A NAME, and bounded: every surface draws `label`, and `min(1)` // alone permits a paragraph — a model surveying a garden named a // corner with a whole sentence, because the prompt is generated // from this file (`graview check`: `label-unbounded`). label: z.string().min(1).max(60), kickOff: z.string(), opponent: z.string(), // Host-kept file ("image"/"video"/"file"); appLinkField() another app // (its records: graview-linked-records); phoneField(), placeField(). crest: imageField().optional(), }), plural: "Fixtures", description: "A match, and the team you intend to put out for it.", edges: { // One edge, two readings: the fixture's page says who is in the // team; the player's page says which fixtures they are picked for. // Kinds sharing an edge name word their own end. "picked-for": { to: ["player"], description: "who is in the team", inverse: "the fixtures they are picked for", }, }, // Its time (`who`: its author): lists, glances, timelines read it. fieldRoles: { when: "kickOff" }, }); ```

**In a document** (`app.json`, `"format": "graview-document"`) it is `kinds.fixture`: `{ "label": "{name}", "fields": { "name": { "type": "string", "required": true } }, "edges": { "pickedFor": { "to": ["player"] } } }`. Kinds are kebab-case (`tool-note`), fields and relations camelCase (`pickedFor`). A choice that takes several of its options at once is `{ "type": "enum", "multiple": true, "options": [...] }` (`z.array(z.enum([...]))`): checkboxes in forms, filtered by one option. Every key, lens and block is in `node_modules/@graview/core/dist/document.schema.json` (its `$schema`).

1. **Add it to `createSchema([...])`.** An edge pointing at a kind that is not in that array is a *typecheck* failure, not a runtime one — `createSchema`'s `ValidateEdgeTargets` sees it.

1. **Say what a node of it is called.** `label` defaults to a `label` field and then to the id. An id in the interface is a bug you shipped, not a placeholder. And say what ONE of the kind is called where its id does not: `noun: "staff member"` on a kind called `staff`, or every sentence about one reads "Change the staff".

An id is still a name a caller may choose: every act that declares `creates: ["fixture"]` takes an optional `id` argument the framework adds, so a seed being synced or an agent that will refer to the node next call gets exactly the id it asked for, or a refusal by name. Never hardcode a bootstrap id — `"today"`, `"u-nick"` — in a mutation body or an invariant; bind a role, a flag or an edge, so a store seeded differently still works. And every kind gets `remove-<kind>` derived, permitted through the acts that create it; every relation `connect-<kind>-<relation>` and `disconnect-` unless your acts do.

1. **Give it verbs.** A kind no mutation names as a subject can have nothing done to it, and the strip says so. Unless you meant that, add a mutation whose `subject.kinds` includes it (the rule shape: `graview-invariant`).

1. **Let the fields be changed, or say why not.** A field you could set at creation, you can change: every settable field no mutation writes is covered by a derived act per kind (`edit-<kind>`, "Change the drill"), editable where it is shown and logged like any other. Two declarations shape it. `writes: ["done"]` on a mutation says which fields it sets when its arguments do not (`finish()` writing `done`) — and a mutation whose argument merely shares a field's name should say `writes: []` (a document's act is read, not guessed); the edit refuses an argument it does not take. A number's bounds (`.int().min(1).max(5)`; a document's `min`, `max`, `step`) bound every form, tool and apply. `fixed: { text: "the client's words, as sent" }` on the kind says a field never changes, and why; the sentence is the documentation. The checker warns `field-without-writer` when a field is still out of everyone's reach, and refuses `writes-unknown-field`, `fixed-unknown-field` and a `fixed-but-written` contradiction.

### Worked examples

`apps/todo/src/domain/schema.ts` (a `rule` kind whose `spec` makes rules data; `fieldRoles` for the timeline); `apps/seedbed/src/domain/schema.ts` (a `lifecycle`: the past is a horizon, not a delete).

### The declarations that keep paying

- **`creates`** on the mutation that adds this kind (`creates: ["fixture"]`): the empty kind card then offers "Add a fixture" by derivation — the blank graph onboards itself, FROM THE ROOT OF THE CHAIN. An act that also takes a `nodeRef` has no candidates on an empty graph, so it is withheld (a picker with nothing in it is worse than no button) and the district says what it is waiting for instead: *"Place a feature" cannot begin until there is a zone.* Expect exactly one way in on a blank installation, and check that it is the one you meant — this only ever shows up on the graph nobody tests against.
- **`fromTheOtherEnd`** on the act that makes or breaks the edge. An act declaring `connects` or `severs` is offered from BOTH ends of the tie, and `title` is written from the subject's side: "Name a caretaker", offered on the gardener, reads as naming hers. Say how it reads standing there (`fromTheOtherEnd: "Take on a plot"`) — `graview check` warns `act-without-far-end-reading` and names the end it has no words for.
- **`display.page`** when a record should not read in declared order: `page: { fields: ["subject", "draft"], groups: [{ title: "Schedule", fields: ["due"] }] }` puts those first, the rest under "Details" (a document's `kinds.<kind>.page`; `{ op: "set-page-fields" }`). A string allowed past 500 characters (`.max(5000)`, a `text`) is prose: full width, paragraphs and lists kept, edited in a text area.
- **`lifecycle`** when members expire — `{ field: "status", retired: ["played"] }` or `{ field: "until", retired: "date" }`. Every count then aggregates over the horizon ("4, +12 past") instead of drowning, and `graview check` refuses a lifecycle reading a missing field.
- **A figure**, line art of the THING at the city's three-quarter angle — a person, a plot of ground, a gutter — drawn wherever the kind is drawn. Nine ship; any domain that is not an abstract tracker runs out of them at once, so draw the rest: `graview figure ./dist/domain/app.js --kind gutter --from "a gutter along a roof edge"` prints the brief (the rules, the angle, a shipped figure as the style), and `--judge <file>` reads the answer back, holds it to the rules `graview check` holds a figure to, and prints the line to paste. Then look at it at twenty pixels, which is the size a chip gives it.
- **A declared hue** in the brand (`accents: { fixture: 210 }`) for a chosen color, not a stable hash: every chip dot, roof and focus tag follows.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build && npx graview check ./dist/domain/app.js
npx graview check --document app.json   # a document
```

Report **the actual output**, including warnings. What it catches here:

- `edge-target-undeclared` — an edge to a kind nobody declared
- `edge-without-inverse` — a relation with words for one of its two readings
- `act-without-far-end-reading` — an act offered on an end it has no words for
- `field-role-missing-field`, `field-role-ill-typed` — a role naming no field; a `when` no date, a `who` no name
- `required-invariant-unregistered` — `requiresInvariant` naming no rule
- `mutation-untitled` / `mutation-undescribed` — a verb nobody can read

### What the check cannot see

Say so rather than implying otherwise:

- Whether the kind is a *kind* at all, or should have been a field on an existing one. The test: does anything point AT it, and does it have a life of its own? A color is a field. A fixture is a kind.
- Whether the default views read well, and the plural in a sentence ("3 Fixtures", never "3 Person"). Run the app and look.

---

Add a node kind to a Graview app — fields, edges, label, plural and field roles — and verify it with graview check rather than claiming it worked.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-node-kind.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-pages-design.html

# graview-pages-design

`graview-pages-design` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Give a Graview app a product design over its routed face — its own shell under the one bar, every surface replaced, its tabs lit from the section a kind's pages are in, and a trail that says where a person is — and verify it by rendering each page and opening it, rather than assuming the derived pages are gone.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## A product design over the pages face

`graview-pages` takes the routed face from derived to one page in the app's own words. This is the rung after: the registry's three surfaces and two page types, all replaced, read as a product rather than an admin panel.

```tsx
createPageRegistry<S, PageComponent<S>>(schema)
  .surface("shell", Shell)        // the design's own, under the bar
  .surface("home", Home)
  .surface("problems", Problems)
  .register("plot", "list", Plots).register("plot", "record", PlotRecord)
  .register("gardener", "list", Gardeners).register("gardener", "record", GardenerRecord)
  .section(["plot", "planting"], "The grounds", { path: "/places/the-grounds" })
  // ... every kind
```

The shell surface receives `{ context, children }`. `apps/todo/src/ui/design.tsx` is the finished example: all a person tries there works: sort, filter and group come from `ArrangeBar` and live in `useSearchParams` in the shared words (a list you arranged is a link); a record edits where it is shown, heading included, through `editableFields(store, id)`; an act's form opens where the act is, prefilled, with the store's own refusal said at the press; the problems page is an inbox, its repairs ordered by `rankedRepairs`; and every empty state offers the way out of itself. `apps/seedbed/src/ui/design.tsx` is the other end: an almanac drawn on the page and in the scene's lens from one model.

### Where a person is

A design usually replaces some pages and leaves the rest derived, and a person who follows a link into a derived page must still know where they are. The face says it; a design never rebuilds it by matching `pluralSlug` against the path.

- **`registry.section(kinds, label, { path })`** names the part of the app a kind's pages belong to — its list, its records, its pictures — as the design's own tabs name it. `path` is the section's own page, basename-relative; without one the trail says the section and links nowhere. `registry.sectionOf(kind)` reads it back.
- **`usePlaceHere()`**, in anything `PagesApp` draws (the shell, a page, a route): `{ as: "home" | "list" | "record" | "place" | "page", kind?, id?, label, section?, trail: [{ label, href?, path?, current? }] }`. Light a tab from `section` (or `kind`), draw a title from `label`. Each step's `href` carries the face's base; `path` is basename-relative, for `<Link to>` and `navigate()`.
- **`placeHere(context, path, { registry, base })`** says the same of a path for a bar drawn OUTSIDE the face's router, told where it is by `steering.at` or `onNavigate`.
- **Its own tabs, in the arrangement's order.** `arrangedEntries(kinds, pages.order, views.places())` (`@graview/core`) is the kinds' lists with a host's view named `view:<name>` at its place among them; leave out a kind `pages.hide` names unless it is where the person is.
- **The trail.** Each derived list, record and picture opens with one: a `nav` called "You are here", the section and the kind's list as links, the page itself last with `aria-current="page"`, out of sight because the heading says it. A list with no section draws none. A shell that places `<PageTrail />` puts THE trail there and the derived pages draw none at their heads; one that draws its own from `usePlaceHere()` says `surface("shell", Shell, { without: ["trail"] })`.

### Find and the way back, in the design's bar

Both are the face's, whichever shell draws it: a shell that places `<PageFind>` or `<PageUndo>` says where they go, else they are drawn around it (Find in a bar above, the way back docked at the corner), and `surface("shell", Shell, { without: ["find", "undo"] })` goes without.

```tsx
<nav className="my-bar">
  <PageFind context={context} narrowsLists={false} size="sm" className="my-find" />
  <PageUndo context={context} compact size="sm" className="my-undo" />
</nav>
```

- **`compact`** is the arrow and "Undo": what it takes back ("Take back “Rename to …”") is its accessible name and its title. Uncompact, the sentence is cut at 18rem (`--graview-undo-widest`), whole in its title.
- **`size`**: `"sm"` (30 px, the app bar's tools), `"md"` (36 px), or the bar's own height — a number of pixels or a CSS length — said as `--graview-control-height`.
- **`className`** goes on Undo's button and on Find's form (its box is `.graview-find-box`). Their own look is rules behind `:where`, so one class of the design's outweighs it: never `!important`, never a CSS `::after` over Undo's words.

### What every design must keep doing

- **Read the graph through one model.** `readGarden(store)` turns nodes, edges and violations into the design's words; every page reads it and none reaches for `store.graph`. The scene's lens reads the same model.
- **Show nothing the graph does not hold.** Copy that changes with the app — a pitch, a chart's tags, a section's words — is records of a kind, seeded, never a JSON file the design imports: `graview check` names a page that reads one (`face-reads-content-beside-the-graph`), and Find, Ask and the scene see records alone.
- **Take the act list from the derivation.** `recordFacts(store, id, { principal }).actions` and `kindFacts(store, kind, …).actions`, never a scan of `store.allMutations()`; `withheld` are struck through with the policy's sentence (`store.permits` says the same at the press), not dropped.
- **Style through the theme's tokens** (`--graview-ground`, `-panel`, `-ink`, `-edge`, `-warn`, `-accent`, `-font-display`, `-font-body`), tinted with `color-mix` for the design's own paper. Never a color that works in one scheme only — nor a logo: `<AppMark brand={context.brand} />` draws the brand's, the dark one in the dark (`graview-logo`).
- **Keep landmarks and targets honest.** One `main` — a `section` when `context.embedded`, and UNNAMED, or a page holding two embeds has two regions with one name. Controls at least 24px, AA contrast. Every size in `rem`: at 200% text a flex or grid item's automatic minimum is its CONTENT's, so one un-wrappable row pushes the whole column off the screen — `minmax(0, 1fr)` and `min-width: 0` on the column, `flex-wrap` on the row. Measure rather than trust: `-ink-faint` fails AA on an 11px label, and the accent fails on the warning ground. `node scripts/verify-pages.mjs` runs axe over every route, both widths, both schemes.
- **Say where a person is on every page, derived or not**, as above — one trail, not one from the design and one from the face.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build && npx graview check ./dist/domain/app.js   # the declaration is still whole
pnpm test                                               # render every page you registered
```

Render each registered page with `PagesApp` and `initialPath` (and the `basename` it ships under) in a test, and assert what `usePlaceHere()` says there and that one `nav[aria-label="You are here"]` is drawn (`apps/seedbed/tests/integration/chapters.test.ts`). Then open it: a design that passes its tests and reads like an admin panel has replaced nothing.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether the design's words are the domain's. The derived pages use the declaration's `description` and `inverse`; a design that writes its own sentences must keep them true as the declaration changes.
- Whether a section's label is the one a person would look for: the trail says what the registry says.
- Whether a page gives every act `facts.actions` offers room: only a person can see that.

---

Give a Graview app a product design over its routed face — its own shell under the one bar, every surface replaced, its tabs lit from the section a kind's pages are in, and a trail that says where a person is — and verify it by rendering each page and opening it, rather than assuming the derived pages are gone.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-pages-design.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-pages.html

# graview-pages

`graview-pages` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Give a Graview app the routed face it wants — from the derived pages, to one page in the app's own words, to the door of a product design that replaces every surface (graview-pages-design).

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## The pages face

A Graview app has two faces over one store. The scene is the picture. The pages face is the same declaration routed as an ordinary web application: a home, a list per kind, a record per node, forms for every act, and a problems page — derived, then replaceable one surface at a time, up to a product design of its own. The ladder ends at the framework's own example: `apps/seedbed`, chapters nine and thirteen.

### What comes for free

```tsx
// main.tsx — one branch: the path decides the face
if (location.pathname.startsWith("/pages")) {
  root.render(<PagesApp basename="/pages" context={{ store, brand, principal, sceneHref: "/" }} />);
}
```

`PagesApp` renders with no registry at all:

- `/` — a GALLERY. The standing as the headline ("2 gardeners, 3 plots and 1 planting." or "Nothing here yet."), then every picture as a large live card, the kinds as a row of counts, a line to the map, and Recently. A kind with no titled lens gets a contact sheet of its members, so a new app lands on a gallery. An empty picture names the act that fills it.
- `/<plural>` — a list per kind, marking trouble, its creating acts beneath.
- `/<plural>/<id>` — a record: its facts, changed where they stand, its relations in the declaration's words, what can be done, what happened.
- `/problems` — every broken rule, with repairs.

The app bar, one row over any shell (`barAbove`): the name, the switch (Scene, Pages; `pages: { scene, pages }` renames them), the place you are on — whose list holds the home, the Lists, the Pictures (standing on a wide bar, else under More, as an empty kind is) — Find, standing, person. A shell with a rail of its own says `surface("shell", Shell, { without: ["places"] })`: the bar keeps all that and names no place. Each list, record and picture opens with a trail (`nav` "You are here": the section, the kind's list, the page itself current), its hrefs under the base.

**Arrange it, declared**: `pages: { order: ["offer", "package"], hide: ["party"], first: "The offers" }`. `order` sorts gallery, nav, city; `hide` keeps kinds off the home and the bar's places (listed only while you are on one), each still at its address and in Find; `first` (place, kind or `"home"`) is where a new visit lands; a drawn home stays Home, on the bar and at `/`. `primary` stands on the bar. `placesOf(app)` (`/seat`) lists them. A lens only a home links to may be `hidden: true` (set-lens-hidden): off the bar and the page list, still at its address; set-lens-hidden on a kind (`title: "party"`) writes `hide`.

**A view the host keeps** (a script view, by its manifest `name`) is `view:<name>` in `order`, `first` and `primary`: listed among the lists where ordered, opened on, stood up. The declaration cannot know the host's views, so `graview check` notes one not registered here ("not drawn here yet") rather than refusing it; a host hands its manifests as `views` to `editDocument` (a title then resolves: `order: ["To do"]` writes `view:to-do`), `compileDocument` and `placesOf(app, { views })`.

**Home as data** (FR-81): `home`, blocks as in `graview-view-specs` (`views.home`), replaces this body, and the app opens on it (FR-136): 40 blocks at its top (a group is one; 120 in all), and a `figure` may say `emphasis: "large"`.

**No home, and `purpose.jobs`** (the face handed `app`): the home opens on the jobs. The first with records waiting is the title, its count, five records, its `act` on each; others follow smaller, an empty one a quiet line, the gallery after. A drawn home answers a job only by listing its kind (`design-job-unanswered`). `composeDesign(document)` (`@graview/core/compose`) proposes jobs (`inferJobs`), the critic's edits and an accent as one change.

**Hand it `views`** (the scene's registry, plus `settings`/`presence`) — `graview create` does — and the face puts the scene's provider under its routes:

- `/places`, `/places/<as>` — every named lens as a page (fullscreen, over the kind's members, the beginning acts beneath unless the lens says `create: false`). A kind's page lists its pictures; a pick in a lens travels to the record. A kind's own row (one × glyph) is each line of its list, and its own page view (one × full) heads its record. A script view that draws its own heading says `heading: "own"` in its manifest: its place then draws no title or count over it.
- `/map` — `kindMap(store)`: every declared relation in its words with its live count, also a section on the home page. A kind's list says what it relates to, arranged in the shared words (`?sort=due:desc`, `?filter=done:false`, `?group=due:month`, `?q=tape`) a lens carries in its fragment, so an arrangement is a link; `?by=`, `?<edge>=<id>`, `?with=` and `?past=1` still land. A record links back.
- `/search?q=` — the Find box's matcher: hits by kind, each with why; a nav box narrows a list, else lands here. Find and the way back ("Take back “…”", ⌘Z) are on every face: a shell places `<PageFind>` or `<PageUndo>` where it wants them, else they are drawn around it (`without: ["find"]` goes without; at a bar's height, `graview-pages-design`).
- **The quick ask** (⌘K, where `ai` gives a model): a bar and answer card by the page's heading, the ROUTE what "this" means. `context.quickAsk: false` draws none.

Everything a page shows is a derivation the scene uses too: `recordFacts`, `deriveAffordances`, `store.permits`. **A page never decides what an act is or who may take it** — it strikes through what the seat may not, and says why. A record's facts, `computed` ones too, read in declared order or as the kind's `display.page` groups them; prose keeps its paragraphs, full width.

**Typed together.** Over a served store, hand the face `typing` (`openRemote`'s `remote.typing`; an embed passes it) and prose is edited live: each keystroke a splice, no Save, others' carets drawn. Markdown, a document's `text` and a string past 500 characters are; a short string is not, and stays a whole value with a Save: a name or a title is changed whole, two people merging letters into one name is a worse name, and a whole write keeps its stale-write check (`markCollaborative` overrides). A keystroke rides an act that writes the field and would run on the record now — its `allowedWhen`, its `allowedOn`, or its `apply` asked — so a record the act refuses is read only to typing too.

**On a phone this face is the answer.** `Shell` carries `pagesHref`.

### Rung one: a page in the app's own words

`createPageRegistry(schema)` replaces pages per kind and surfaces per app:

```tsx
import { createPageRegistry, DerivedForm, kindFacts, PageMain, pageStyles, recordFacts, SceneLink, useStoreTick } from "@graview/pages";

function PlotPage({ context }: { context: PageContext<S> }) {
  const { store, principal } = context;
  useStoreTick(store);                                   // re-render on every op
  const id = decodeURIComponent(useParams()["id"] ?? "");
  const facts = recordFacts(store, id, { principal });   // the same derivations
  return (
    <PageMain context={context}>
      <h1 style={pageStyles.h1}>{facts.label}</h1>
      <SceneLink context={context} stop={`#focus=${id}`} />
      <DerivedForm store={store} mutation={sow} prefilled={{ plotId: id }} />
    </PageMain>
  );
}

export const pages = createPageRegistry<S, PageComponent<S>>(schema)
  .register("plot", "record", PlotPage)
  .route("/survey", SurveyDesk);   // about nothing in the schema
```

**Claim a declared block, keep the rest.** A block may say `"key": "rewrites"` (unsaid, its sort and place: `list.2`); `<BlockSlots.Provider value={{ "change.page": { rewrites: Timeline } }}>` draws yours for it and every other block as declared; a blocks lens is claimed by its address (`"the-offers"`). Never pick a block by its title's words.

`.route(path, Component)` gives a page that is NOT about a kind an address — onboarding, settings, import — matched before `/:plural`. **Every `to` is basename-relative** (`to="/survey"`, never `to="/pages/survey"`), and so is `initialPath`, so a test renders the hrefs a browser will.

Rules for a page at this rung:

1. **`PageMain`, not `<main>`** — inside an embed the host owns the one `main`, and a hand-written one is a duplicate landmark.
2. **`useStoreTick(store)`** at the top of every page that reads the graph, or it goes stale after the first act.
3. **`pageStyles`** for the parts you did not design: one face, derived or not.
4. **Prefill, never wire.** `DerivedForm` with `prefilled` is how a record offers an act about itself; the form asks for the rest.
5. **Read permission before drawing an act.** `store.permits({ name, args }, principal)`, struck through with `verdict.refusal.message`. A form that refuses on submit is the bug this prevents.
6. **Link to a PICTURE, not only to a node.** `spatialHref(id)` opens the scene on one thing; `placeHref(as)` (`/#view=the-grounds`) on one named place. A scene not at `/`: set `sceneHref` in the PagesApp context; both take it second.
7. **Take the act LIST from the derivation, not from the mutations.** `recordFacts(store, id, { principal }).actions` is the `AffordanceSet` the scene's strip reads: `affordances` can act here, `args` decided and `open` questions left; `withheld` are this seat's refusals, with the reason. `store.allMutations()` offers acts with nothing to act on. A **list** page asks it of a kind instead — `kindFacts(store, kind, { principal }).actions`, the acts that can BEGIN it.

### Rung two: a product design

Replacing every surface — the shell under the bar, the home, the problems, each kind's list and record — is a product: `graview-pages-design`, with its own tabs lit from the section a kind's pages are in, and Find and the way back in its own bar.

### On somebody else's page

`graview-embed` mounts the app, this face included (`face: "pages"`, `path`, `routing`), into one element of any page.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build && npx graview check ./dist/domain/app.js   # the declaration is still whole
pnpm test                                               # render every page you registered
```

Render each registered page with `PagesApp` and `initialPath` in a test (`apps/seedbed/tests/integration/chapters.test.ts`). Then open it: a design that passes its tests and reads like an admin panel has replaced nothing.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether the design's words are the domain's. The derived pages use the declaration's `description` and `inverse`; a design that writes its own sentences must keep them true as the declaration changes.
- Whether a page gives every act `facts.actions` offers room: only a person can see that.

---

Give a Graview app the routed face it wants — from the derived pages, to one page in the app's own words, to the door of a product design that replaces every surface (graview-pages-design).

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-pages.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-permissions.html

# graview-permissions

`graview-permissions` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Declare who may do what in a Graview app once, so the store enforces it, the actions strip narrows and an agent seat narrows with it — verified by graview check and by trying it.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Declare who may do what

Permission is another input to a derivation the framework already does. What can be done is already DERIVED from the schema and the invariants, so adding a principal and some grants narrows the interface and the agent surface at the same time, from one declaration.

Two things must not be got wrong, and they are the reason to follow this rather than improvise.

**Enforcement belongs at the STORE.** The tool runtime calls the same mutations a person does, so a check inside a React component is not a permission system, it is a suggestion — and the agent seat is the bypass.

**An action you may not take should SAY SO rather than vanish.** Hiding it teaches people the software is broken: they watched a colleague do this yesterday and now the button is gone.

### Do this

1. **Write the policy where the checker can read it.** In your domain layer, not your UI:

```ts export const policy: Policy = { roles: ["coach", "analyst", "player"], grants: [ { roles: ["coach"], mutations: "*" }, { roles: ["analyst"], mutations: ["plan-drill", "cut-drill", "design-drill"] }, // The line can be drawn by SUBJECT KIND on the same mutation: an // analyst may rename a drill and not a position, because a position's // name is part of the formation and the formation is selection. { roles: ["analyst"], mutations: ["rename"], kinds: ["drill", "session"] }, { roles: ["player"], mutations: ["end-unavailability", "explain"] }, ], }; ```

1. **Hand it to both `defineApp` and the `Store`.** `defineApp` is what `graview check` reads; the `Store` is what enforces.

The derived acts ride your grants rather than needing their own line: `edit-<kind>` is permitted to whoever may change or make the kind, and `remove-<kind>`, `archive-<kind>`, `unarchive-<kind>` and `merge-<kind>` to whoever may make it — but only over the records that seat made. To take out anybody's, name the act in the grant or say `*`. A grant to every role (`roles: "*"`) is a door, not a key: riding only it, even the edit reaches just the seat's own records, so "anybody may join" lets each person change or remove their own record, never everybody's. A relation's derived `connect-<kind>-<relation>` and `disconnect-<kind>-<relation>` ride the edit's reading, on the kind the relation leaves. A refusal names who could, so a seat told no learns what it lacks rather than concluding the capability is missing.

1. **Give the provider a principal.** `<GraviewProvider principal={{ kind: "human", id: me.id, roles: me.roles }}>`. The interface reads it to decide what to OFFER; the store decides what to allow; the log attributes to it. Three readings of one object, which is why they cannot drift.

1. **Do not filter anything yourself.** The narrowing happens once, in `deriveAffordances`. A provider written tomorrow inherits it.

1. **Remember the absence of a policy permits everything.** That keeps permission opt-in rather than a tax every app pays before it has decided it has users.

1. **The derived edits ride your grants.** `edit-<kind>` — the act the framework derives for fields nobody writes — is permitted to whoever may already run an act that writes a field of that kind or creates one, on that kind. An analyst who may `resize-drill` may change a drill's other fields; a player who may not, may not. Nothing to add to the policy; a grant may still name `edit-drill` outright, and `*` reaches it. When no role may write or create a kind at all, `graview check` says so per field (`field-without-writer`): grant an act, or mark the field `fixed`.

1. **Put the installation in the graph.** Who may use the app, who has been asked to, and what each holds are nodes and acts, not a second app:

```ts const installation = declareInstallation({ roles: ["coach", "analyst", "player"], admin: "coach" }); createSchema([...yours, ...installation.kinds]); // user, invitation — typed, so // an edge may say to: ["user"] mutations: [...yours, ...installation.mutations]; // invite, welcome, remove-user, grant, revoke, revoke-invitation modules: installation.modules; // drawn only for those who administer it policy: installation.withPolicy(policy); // the admin's grants, and "you, on yours" for a profile ```

The coach sees "Show the installation" in the person's menu on the app bar and the people and invitations rise as ordinary districts; nobody else ever sees them. A person's record page is their profile, and the derived `edit-user` is theirs alone through a `self: true` grant. Register `reachLens` over the people with a title and the policy is a picture: roles down the side, acts across the top, a mark where the store would say yes. Chapter 14 of `apps/seedbed` is the worked example.

**Pointing at a person?** `declareInstallation({ …, required: true })`. An edge into a module the app can turn off earns a `module-edge-leak` warning, and for people the only answer is "it is never off" — an installation without people is a household of one, not a disabled module. Say it once and the checker stops asking.

1. **Say who sees what, for every kind — and which fields.** `sees` keeps records (and, with `hide` or `fields`, some of their fields) from seats the way grants keep acts. It is a job of its own: the `graview-sight` skill.

1. **Say which kind is the people.** `people: true` on one kind (a document's `"people": true`; the installation's `user` says it): a record of it whose id is a principal's id IS that person. Then: - `{ roles: ["participant"], kinds: ["match"], via: "givenBy" }` shows a seat a match only where `givenBy` joins it to their own record — each Secret Santa giver sees their match, not the one they receive in (`own` would show both). - `{ mutations: ["take-back"], ownEnd: true }` holds a connect or sever to the seat's own end of the link: a voter takes back their own vote. Every link the act touches is held, so a connect on a relation of one that would replace somebody else's is refused. - A document act's `"to": "$me"` (or `"set": { "champion": "$me" }`) is the acting person's record — the tool stops asking who, a seat with no record is refused with a sentence, and only that person can undo it. - A document says each by a named edit, previewed in words: `set-people` (`kind`, `people`), `add-grant` / `remove-grant`, `add-sight` / `remove-sight` (a removal names it by roles and acts or kinds).

1. **Open one act to people with no account.** An RSVP or a sign-up is a grant to a `visitor` role the host mints per answer, a sight that never names it, and `forms.<name>` saying the act: the `graview-visitor-forms` skill.

### Worked examples

- `packages/core/tests/unit/permissions.test.ts` — grants by role, by mutation and by subject kind, and the refusal that names who could
- `packages/tools/tests/unit/affordances.test.ts` — a guarded store: what a principal is offered, what is withheld and said, and how the agent seat narrows with it
- `packages/core/tests/document/fixtures/secret-santa.gdd.json` and `idea-board.gdd.json` — a sight via a relation, `$me` and an own-end grant

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build && npx graview check ./dist/domain/app.js
```

The checker reports `mutation-unreachable-by-any-role` (declared and unreachable), `role-may-do-nothing` (a role that can neither run a mutation nor see a kind; a viewer that only reads is not reported, since reading is the point of it), `grant-unknown-mutation` and `grant-unknown-kind`. All four are silent at runtime and obvious at build time, and the person who finds them otherwise is the person standing in front of a button they cannot press. Report the output. The people have theirs: `people-ambiguous` (two kinds say it), `people-unsaid` (a `via`, an `ownEnd` or a `$me` and no people kind), `sight-via-misses-people` (a relation that never reaches them) and `grant-own-end-without-link`.

What a sight keeps, and the checks that say so (`act-reads-hidden-kind`, `rule-says-hidden-fact`, the `sight-*` codes), are `graview-sight`'s.

**And try it.** Two tests that matter more than the check:

```ts
it("refuses at the store, where nothing can go around it", () => {
  expect(() => store.apply(call, { author: player })).toThrow(PermissionDeniedError);
  expect(store.log.length).toBe(0);
});

it("narrows the agent seat from the same policy", () => {
  const seat = createToolRuntime(store, { author: { kind: "agent", roles: ["player"] } });
  expect(seat.definitions.map((t) => t.name)).not.toContain("select-player");
});
```

Undo is a change and is judged like one: what you may undo is what you may have done. If you have a custom undo path, check it goes through `store.undo`.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether the roles match how the organization actually works. That is a conversation, not a declaration.
- Whether a withheld action's message helps. It names the roles that could; whether that is useful depends on whether a person knows who holds them.
- Whether the principal is who they say they are. Graview authorizes; it does not authenticate. Wire that to your own identity provider and pass the result in as the principal.

---

Declare who may do what in a Graview app once, so the store enforces it, the actions strip narrows and an agent seat narrows with it — verified by graview check and by trying it.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-permissions.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-port-app.html

# graview-port-app

`graview-port-app` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Port an existing application onto Graview — deciding what is a node, what is a field and what is an edge — and proving the port with a parity test rather than an assertion.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Port an existing application

The hard part of a port is not the code. It is deciding what your existing schema was really saying, because a relational schema hides three different things inside a foreign key: a real relationship, an implementation detail, and a thing that should have been a node all along.

### The decisions, in order

1. **What is a NODE?** The test: does anything point at it, and does it have a life of its own? A `status` string is a field. A `rationale` — a reason someone recorded, that outlives the person who recorded it and that other things refer to — is a node, and turning it into one is usually the moment a port starts paying for itself.

1. **What is an EDGE?** A relationship a person would name out loud. `assigned-to` is an edge. `created_at` is a field. A join table with columns on it is a node, not an edge, and pretending otherwise is the mistake that costs most later.

1. **What is a MUTATION?** Every change, named as an act rather than as a write. Not `updateDuty` but "Reassign run". The title is the label a person reads in the strip AND the instruction an agent reads in its tool schema, so an opaque one costs twice. If you find yourself writing `patch`, you have skipped this step.

1. **What is an INVARIANT?** Everything your current code validates, plus everything it was supposed to. Give each one repairs — see `graview-invariant`. Rules that name their repairs are where the interface stops needing you to design it.

1. **What is a LENS?** Your primary screen, described without your nouns. A calendar is intervals in columns. A checklist grid is a bipartite mapping. A formation is positions with domain-given coordinates. If one of the three shipped lenses fits, bind roles to your fields and write no picture at all.
