1. **What is CONTENT?** Everything a page shows — a pitch's sections, a chart's tags, the words of a section — is records of a kind, seeded, never a JSON file a view imports beside the graph: the scene, Find, the record pages and Ask see records and nothing else. `graview check` names a face module that reads one (`face-reads-content-beside-the-graph`).

### Do this

1. Build the domain tier first, with no UI. Get `graview check` clean before anything renders.
2. Load your real data through a `snapshot`, not a fixture you invented. A port that works on twelve made-up nodes and falls over on the real graph has proved nothing.
3. Register default views, look at it, and only then write custom ones.
4. Port the rules LAST, and port them as tests first.

### Worked example

- The household product (now in its own repository) is a port. Its parity fixture was generated by running the ORIGINAL app's code over the same data, and its test asserts the framework's invariants reproduce every violation — 90 across 9 provocations. That fixture-and-test pair is the reason anyone should believe a port, and the shape to copy.

### If the port is a document

A system that emits its own projection — an adapter writing a `graview-document@1` JSON and a snapshot, with a face of your own over it — gets the compiler's help in three places, and should take all three:

1. **Name the schema.** `"$schema": "./node_modules/@graview/core/dist/document.schema.json"` at the top of the document: the editor then flags an unknown key as you type (a `fieldRoles` the format does not have) instead of `graview check` refusing it later. The schema is generated from the compiler's own shape, one per version.
2. **Or write it in TypeScript.** `defineDocument({...})` from `@graview/core/typed` returns the same JSON; a key the format lacks, an edge to an undeclared kind, a glance field the kind lacks or a relation an act connects that nobody declares is a type error. Expressions stay strings.
3. **Read the store through its types.** `npx graview types n.graview.json --out src/document.d.ts`, then `typedReader<Types>(store)`: `fieldOf(task, "status")` is the enum's options, `edgesOf(task, "under")` the kinds it reaches. Never `Record<string, unknown>` and `typeof` checks: a renamed relation must fail `tsc`, not draw a blank section. Regenerate in the build so it cannot drift.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build && npx graview check ./dist/domain/app.js
```

**And write the parity test.** This is the one thing that makes a port trustworthy, and it is worth more than every other check here combined: run the OLD system's validation and the new invariants over the same graphs, and assert they agree.

```ts
// Generated by running the old code over N provocations, then committed.
import expected from "./fixtures/legacy-violations.json";

it("agrees with the system it replaces, violation for violation", () => {
  for (const provocation of provocations) {
    const store = createStore({ snapshot: provocation.graph });
    const mine = store.violations().map((v) => v.message).sort();
    expect(mine).toEqual(expected[provocation.name]);
  }
});
```

The framework's own the household example port does this across 90 violations and nine provocations, against a fixture generated by running the original code. If you cannot generate that fixture, say so — and say what you are relying on instead, because "I read both and they look the same" is a different claim.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether you modeled the domain or transcribed the database. The symptom is edges named after columns.
- Whether behavior the old system had is gone. Only the parity test knows.
- Whether the port is worth finishing. A port that has not made anything clearer by the third kind is telling you something.

---

Port an existing application onto Graview — deciding what is a node, what is a field and what is an edge — and proving the port with a parity test rather than an assertion.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-port-app.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-seed.html

# graview-seed

`graview-seed` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Get a Graview app from a blank graph to a useful one — the order the declaration already states, a plan a model proposes, and one turn that can be taken back.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Fill a blank graph

Every product ships empty once, and it is the state its author never sees: your own graph has had data in it since the first afternoon. A ten-kind app on a blank installation is one door and nine silent districts, and the person who finds that out is the first one to open it.

Two things make it a surface rather than a wall: the app already declares the ORDER things must be made in, and what a model proposes can be an object rather than a list of calls somebody applies by hand.

### What the declaration already says

`creates: ["feature"]` on an act, and `zoneId: nodeRef(["zone"])` in its input, are together a chain: a feature cannot be made until a zone exists.

```ts
import { beginning } from "@graview/core/seat";
const chain = beginning(app);
chain.roots;        // kinds that can begin with nothing in the graph
chain.doors;        // the acts that are the way in
chain.order;        // every kind, with what it waits for and how deep
chain.unreachable;  // what nothing here can make — often right, always worth seeing
```

`graview check` says it as a note (`blank-graph-unreachable`), and `graview describe` reads the whole thing out. Run it before you believe your app onboards anybody:

```sh
pnpm build:domain && npx graview describe ./dist/domain/app.js
```

### Do this

1. **Mount `<Begin>`.** It is derived — the chain, the acts that can run now, what everything else is waiting for, in your own plurals. Put it on the home surface of the routed face, or anywhere a person lands first. It stands down on its own once every kind has something in it: ```tsx <Begin whenFull={<YourOwnHome />} /> ```

1. **Give the root kind an act that needs nothing.** One act with no required `nodeRef` is the difference between an app that onboards itself and one that cannot be started. If every creating act needs a node, `graview check` says `blank-graph-has-no-door` — and if the data really arrives by seed, migration or sync, that note is the answer rather than a fault.

1. **Let a model propose, and make it a plan.** A plan is ordered by the chain, judged before any of it runs, reviewable, and applied as ONE turn: ```ts import { applyPlan, planFrom } from "@graview/tools"; const plan = planFrom(store, proposals, { app, principal }); const done = applyPlan(store, plan, { author: surveyor }); store.undo(done.batch); // the whole seeding, back the way it arrived ``` A call can name what it is about to make — `as: "lawn"` — and a later call points at it with `{ $plan: "lawn" }`. That is the only way a model can refer to a node that does not exist yet, and it is what turns forty proposals into one graph. It is all-or-nothing and says where it stopped; `keepWhatRan` is for a caller who would rather have the half.

1. **Show it before you run it.** `<PlanReview plan={plan} declinable />` draws the plan in the order it will run, counts what it makes, and strikes refusals through with their reason. `declinable` lets a person drop one — and declining the area declines the tree standing in it, said beside the entry BEFORE the press (`dependentsOf`, `without`). A seeding nobody read is a seeding nobody can trust, and a review nobody can disagree with is not a review.

1. **If the data is already a spreadsheet, import it, don't retype it.** `importRows(store, kind, rows, mapping, { by })` (`@graview/core/import`) reads each cell by its field's type, links a cell to a record by its name, lands one undoable batch and says each refused row in words; offer `proposeMapping` and `previewImport` first. Import the far ends (events) before the kind that names them (vendors). Imported again, pass `match: "label"` (or `{ column, field }`): a row changes the record it finds, through its edit act, instead of making a second. See `docs/import.md`.

1. **Write the prompt from the graph, not from your head.** The model needs the kinds, the acts and their arguments — which `generateLlmsTxt(app)` (`@graview/core/check`) already writes — plus what is already there, so it does not propose a second Back Lawn.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build:domain && npx graview check ./dist/domain/app.js
npx graview describe ./dist/domain/app.js
```

A document (`app.json`, a graview-document) needs no build: `npx graview describe --document app.json` reads the same chain out, and `npx graview preview app.json --seed seed.json` serves the scene and Pages over a snapshot (`{ "nodes": [{ "id", "kind", …fields }], "edges": [{ "kind", "from", "to" }] }`) so you can walk in as a person would.

Then open it with an empty store (Start fresh, with a ship browser adapter) and go through your own front door. A test holds it: derive the affordances of each root kind on an empty graph and assert the way in is offered, and that a kind deeper in the chain offers nothing and says what it waits for.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether the order is the order a PERSON would want. The chain says what is possible, not what is kind: an app may be able to start with practices and still want to ask about the ground first.
- Whether the model's proposals are any good. They are typed, ordered, permitted and reversible — none of which makes them right, which is why the review is a surface and not a formality.
- Whether a seeded graph reads as somebody's. Ten plausible rows a model invented look exactly like ten rows that matter, until someone reads them.

---

Get a Graview app from a blank graph to a useful one — the order the declaration already states, a plan a model proposes, and one turn that can be taken back.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-seed.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-ship.html

# graview-ship

`graview-ship` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Deploy a Graview app — persistence, op-log-native migrations, export and health — with one declaration and one adapter, self-hosted or behind a service.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Ship a Graview app

`@graview/ship` holds what every deployment needs. One `defineApp` declaration plus one persistence adapter is a running deployment; nothing here requires a service. A graph projected from another system, synced back to it, or kept in step with a Google calendar is `graview-sync`.

### Do this

1. **Open the store through ship**, not by hand:

```ts import { createFileAdapter, openStore } from "@graview/ship";

const opened = await openStore({ app, adapter: createFileAdapter("./data") }); // opened.store is an ordinary Store; every applied diff is appended to // the log and the snapshot rewritten, serialized in order. Hand off with // `await opened.flush()` before close/exit — writes are async. // One writer per scope: opening it twice interleaves and clobbers. ```

The file adapter is deliberately readable: `snapshot.json`, append-only `log.jsonl`, `meta.json` with the stored schema version. The core's sqlite adapter is the scale answer.

**In the page, with no server**, the browser adapter stores the same three things in IndexedDB (localStorage only where IndexedDB will not open; a store localStorage already holds is carried forward on its first open). An edit is kept when `apply` returns, not when IndexedDB commits: a journal in localStorage holds what IndexedDB has not yet, and the next open puts it back, so a page left at once loses nothing. It slots into the same call — import it from `@graview/ship/browser` so the bundler never meets `node:fs`:

```ts import { browserStartsFresh, createBrowserAdapter, forgetFreshParam, openStore } from "@graview/ship/browser";

const opened = await openStore({ app, adapter: createBrowserAdapter(), seed, fresh: browserStartsFresh(), // Start fresh (freshHref) asks; a driven browser gets it unless ?remember=1 }); forgetFreshParam(); // the seed is the FIRST load, not every load ```

Reopened, the store carries its persisted history: earlier edits are in the activity, attributed, and undoable. Give the person a visible way back — `StartFresh` from `@graview/primitives`, or `remembers: true` on the pages context — because a demo that can be edited into a corner with no exit teaches distrust. The sample apps' `main.tsx` files are the worked examples; `pnpm remember` is the harness that holds them to it.

**The seed is read once**, into an empty store. When the default content moves afterwards, do not delete the store to see it — diff and land it:

```sh graview sync-seed ./dist/domain/app.js --seed ./src/data/example.json --data ./data graview sync-seed ./dist/domain/app.js --seed ./src/data/example.json --data ./data --apply ```

The first prints the content steps — `task t-van is put`, `today is patched: label`, `today holds t-van is tied` — and writes nothing, or exits 1 naming every record, field and declared limit the store would refuse (`Step: Too big: expected number to be <=4`); the second lands them as one operation authored `system · ship:sync-seed`, logged, undoable, leaving what people made alone unless `--prune` says otherwise. The same five steps (`put-node`, `patch-node`, `drop-node`, `put-edge`, `drop-edge`) go in `migrations[]` through `stepsMigration` when every installation should get them.

1. **Version the declaration, and migrate in primitives.** When the schema changes shape:

```ts defineApp({ ..., version: 2, migrations: [{ from: 1, to: 2, title: "size words become bed counts", apply: (snapshot) => snapshot.nodes .filter((node) => node.kind === "plot") .map((node) => ({ op: "patch-node", id: node.id, before: { size: node.size, beds: undefined }, after: { size: undefined, beds: node.size === "large" ? 6 : 2 } })), }], }) ```

A migration answers in the op log's own five words, so running one appends ordinary operations — authored `system · ship:migration`, stating intent, undone like any other. `openStore` runs the pending chain on load. `graview check` refuses a chain with a hole or a multi-version jump (`migration-gap`, `migration-not-single-step`) before deploy time finds it.

1. **Export is the exit.** `exportBundle(app, store)` — graph, attributed history and version in one JSON shape; `assertBundle` refuses someone else's app or a newer version, plainly. A tenant who cannot leave was never a customer.

1. **Health is coherence, not liveness.** `health(store)` reports sizes, standing and dangling edges — poll it per deployment, curl it self-hosted.

**Files are yours to store.** An `image`/`file` field keeps a `FileValue`; its `href` is your path. Hand `mount` `files: { upload, maxBytes, kinds }` (dev: `devFiles()`; under a base, `filesAt(base + "/graview/files")`). Serve each as its bytes' type, `nosniff`, a `sandbox` CSP on all but a PDF (an SVG runs script otherwise), only to a seat that `seesId` a record holding it. A page with a CSP allows the files route in `object-src`, or a PDF is its one line, Open / Download, and no box.

1. **Serve it, and let an agent in.** `graview serve <entry> --data ./data` puts the store behind HTTP with the op log as the wire; `graview mcp <entry> --remote-url <url>` and `graview apply … --remote-url <url>` are the same commands an agent uses against a folder, now against the server, judged under the seat the request carries. Put `serve` and `mcp` in the app's scripts. The routes are `WIRE`, exported and pinned by a test, and `serveStore({ seatOf })` is where a host reads its own credential from the `Request` — `openRemote({ headers })` carries whatever it asks for. Off Node (a Worker, a Durable Object, Deno), `createStoreHandler` from `@graview/ship/runtime` answers the same routes as `handle(request)`. A store believes the seat headers the framework's clients send only with `trustSeatHeaders: true` (`graview serve` sets it on 127.0.0.1 and refuses another `--host` without `--trust-seat-headers`); with neither, it answers 401. On 127.0.0.1 it answers only its own origin, and a page on another one `--allow-origin` names (a dev server's app that opens the store with `openRemote`), and no header there names the system's seat. Each run there mints a key and believes only a request carrying it, so another account on the machine cannot claim a seat: hand `openRemote`, `--remote-url` and a page's own server parameter the address it printed, whole (`?graview_key=…`); health answers without it.

1. **A host serving document apps compiles once, on the server.** Send `serializeCompiled(compileDocument(document))` beside the document, and build the app in the page with `appFromOrCompile({ compiled, document })` from `@graview/core/compiled` — never `@graview/core/document`, which brings the compiler back into the first chunk. A compiled app of another format (`graview-compiled@1` today), or made from another document than the one beside it, is not built and the document is compiled instead; `pnpm verify hosted` says what the page carries.

1. **Look at a document with no product.** `graview preview <document.json> --seed <snapshot.json>` is `serve` with Graview's own faces over the store — the scene and Pages, in memory unless `--data` says where, which it then holds: `sync-seed --apply` and `apply` refuse until it stops (Ctrl-C or `kill` stops it within seconds, open pages or not; a hold whose process died is taken over, and says so) — and `graview shots … --places home,overview --out shots` photographs named places headless (Playwright is yours to install). Like `serve`, each preview run mints a key and every address it prints carries it: open one of those, since nothing but health answers without it. Prove a change to an emitted document with these, not hand-written screenshots. In a test, `compileDocumentFiles(path, { seed })` from `@graview/core/testing` reads the document where it lives — no fixture copy to drift.

1. **Edits reach readers when published, if you say so.** `publishing: { mode: "on-publish", working: ["editor"] }` on the declaration (absent, `"live"`: as they are made). The working roles, and an agent acting for one, edit the head live; every other seat — a visitor, an embed, a static page, a linked read — is served the last publish. A publisher (`publishers`, else `working`) runs the built-in `publish` act; undoing it takes readers back. Writes always land on the head: a visitor's answer reaches readers with the next publish. `?as=published` shows a collaborator what readers see, and `unpublished(store)` from `@graview/core/history` says what is waiting. A server loads `@graview/core/publishing` (ship does). Hand `app.publishing` to any store you make yourself — `openStore` and the embed do — and prove it by opening the app as a visitor.

### Then find out whether it worked

Write, close, reopen, and read: the graph must survive the round trip and the persisted log must carry your ops with their authors. The framework's own rehearsal (`pnpm smoke`) does exactly this from packed tarballs — `theDeploymentShipped` is the verdict to mimic.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether your migration is the RIGHT transform — the chain being unbroken says nothing about the data arriving meaningful. Migrate a copy of real data and read it before shipping the step.
- Whether the adapter's storage location survives your deployment story (containers with ephemeral disks lose a file adapter's whole point).
- Whether the export round-trips: rehearse an import into a fresh deployment, the way the framework's smoke run does — do not assume it.

### The boundary

Anything ONE deployment needs belongs in ship: the op log, the snapshot, migrating on open, the wire, a principal on every apply, the seed at first install, content steps, the agent's door on the dev server (`localIntelligence`, taught in `graview-desk`), connections (`graview-sync`). Tenancy, provisioning, billing, quotas and fleet upgrades belong to the operator of many — a service consuming ship like any customer, with its own `seatOf` mapping people and keys to principals. The concern table is in `@graview/ship`'s README; a third party can stand up their own host from it without forking anything.

---

Deploy a Graview app — persistence, op-log-native migrations, export and health — with one declaration and one adapter, self-hosted or behind a service.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-ship.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-shipped-lens.html

# graview-shipped-lens

`graview-shipped-lens` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Declare one of the lenses Graview ships — a calendar, a status board, a coverage, a timeline, a board, a plan, a blocks place — as a titled place with its bindings and options, and read what graview check and add-lens refuse (an option the lens does not take, a lens that cannot draw, a title taken) rather than drawing a lens that quietly ignores a key.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Declare a shipped lens

Most pictures an app wants are already written. A `lenses` entry with a `title` is a PLACE the framework draws with no registration — a tab, a name on its district, a page at `/places/<as>`:

```ts
lenses: [
  { name: "calendar", title: "The month", bindings: { task: { start: "due" } }, options: { range: "month" } },
  { name: "columns", title: "The board", bindings: { task: { column: "status" } }, options: { cap: 50 } },
]
```

Writing a lens of your own, one that binds roles so another domain can reuse it, is `graview-lens`. **Declare before you write**: a shipped lens is data, so a document, a chat and `add-lens` can all say it.

### The lenses and what each takes

`options` are data, and each lens takes only its own (`SHIPPED_LENSES[name].options` on `@graview/core`); read that table rather than guessing a key:

| Lens | Binds | Roles | Options |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `timeline` | fields | `start`, `end` | `columns`, `extent`, `tick`, `minWindow`, `arranging` |
| `calendar` | fields | `start` | `today`, `range`, `weekStartsOn`, `perCell`, `horizon`, `arranging`, `search`, `filters` |
| `columns` | fields | `column` | `sort`, `search`, `filters`, `move`, `collapsed`, `cap`, `hidden` |
| `coverage` | entities | `rows`, `columns`, `link` | `rowRef`, `rowGroup`, `groupOrder`, `requiredGroups`, `requiredVia`, `badge`, `columnGroup`, `sort`, `columnSort`, `search`, `filters` |
| `board` | entities | `slots`, `x`, `y`, `fill` | `fillFrom`, `slotCode`, `zones`, `aspect`, `emptyLabel`, `pickTarget`, `arranging`, `arrange` |
| `plan` | entities | `regions`, `outline` | `hues`, `aspect`, `undrawnLabel`, `strayLabel`, `draw`, `place`, `help` |
| `reach` | nothing | — | — |
| `blocks` | nothing | — | `blocks` |

A **fields** lens binds a kind's own fields onto its roles (`bindings: { task: { start: "due" } }`); an **entities** lens binds roles onto whole kinds and edges (`{ rows: { kind: "skill" }, columns: { kind: "person" }, link: { edge: "develops" } }`). `on` names the kind a place stands on when the bindings do not (reach; a coverage over its columns).

- **A status board** (`columns`) draws a kind's records in columns by one choice field, in its declared order. A card moves only by an act setting that field (`book` where its `allowedWhen` holds): dragged, carried by the keyboard (Space, arrows, Space) or from its menu's "Move to ›". `search` names the fields Find looks in (past 20 cards Find shows unasked), `filters` the chips, `collapsed` columns open shut, `hidden` ones are not drawn, `cap` keeps each column to its newest (1 to 500), and `move: true` puts a Move button under each card.
- **A calendar** opens at `range` — `day`, `week`, `month`, `quarter`, `year`, `years` or `agenda` — on `today` (`"YYYY-MM-DD"`, else the day it is drawn). `range: "years"` with `horizon: { years: 30, title: "The career" }` spans its records, first to last, as well as `years` from `today`; `from` and `to` (years: 1962, 2023) pin its ends.
- **A timeline** needs columns: named in `columns`, or read from the choices of the field its `column` role is bound to.
- **A coverage**'s `sort` orders its rows and `columnSort` its columns; a status board's `sort` orders its cards: a field or `{ by, direction }`, `label` the name, held to the kind. A coverage with no columns, or no link over its relation, says so ("No genres yet: link songs to genres.") and lists no rows.
- **A blocks place** is drawn from the closed block set (headline, figure, list — `graview-view-specs`), each record by its own row or card: `{ name: "blocks", title: "What we heard", on: "signal", options: { blocks: [{ list: "all('signal')", group: "type", as: "row" }] } }`. Nothing in it runs; a chat can write it. Write code only for what blocks cannot say: a grid of cells, positions. Its page already has a header: the place's title, then a line (how many it holds), then "All … as a list →". Do not open with a headline repeating either. A first `headline` becomes that line, in place of the count, and is not drawn again; open with `text` for an intro. Groups head with label and count, rows sit on the title's edge, and a row's `{status} · {type} · on {date}` draws its choices as chips.

Any titled place may say `create: false` when it is read, not written (its page drops the forms that add one), `hidden: true` to keep it off the lists while it stays a link target, and `arrangedBy` in the grammar (`{ group: "held-at" }`) for how it opens, held to the bound kind.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build && npx graview check ./dist/domain/app.js
```

The checker holds every titled lens and says, at its path, what it will not draw and what it ignores:

- `lens-option-unknown` — a key the lens does not take, in one sentence and its fix: "The columns lens takes no option "shade", so "Work" ignores it." / "Use one of: sort, search, filters, move, collapsed, cap, hidden." A declaration carrying one still compiles, with the warning; **`add-lens` refuses it** at `edits.<i>.options.<key>`, and a change sent as a JSON patch or a whole document is judged by `lensOptionsRefused(stored, proposed)` (`@graview/core/document`): an error for each such key the same lens did not already carry.
- `lens-cannot-draw` — it binds no kind, its board's column field is not a choice, its timeline has no columns, its calendar's `today` is not a date or its `range` not one it opens at, it stands on what is not a kind, or its title has nothing to make an address of.
- `lens-not-shipped` — a title on a lens the framework does not draw; `lens-title-taken` — two pictures on one kind under one title. `add-lens` names the lens that holds the title, hidden or not (hiding frees no title); `"replace": "<that title>"` draws yours in its place, kept off the lists if that one was, until set-lens-hidden shows it; `lens-options-not-an-object`, `lens-sort`, `lens-horizon`, `lens-create` and `lens-hidden-untitled` say the rest.
- The bindings themselves: `lens-role-unbound`, `lens-binding-missing-field` and `lens-binding-undeclared-kind`.

`graview describe` lists the places that draw, saying which are hidden. Report the output, then open each place on both faces and look.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether the place is the right picture. A calendar of what has no date that matters, or a board over a field nobody moves, draws without a finding; open it and ask whether a person would reach for it.
- Whether its options read well. `cap`, `collapsed` and `sort` are held to the kind, not to what a person needs first; look at it full.
- Whether a card can be moved by the seat who needs to. The board moves by the acts the seat may run; sit as them and try it (`graview-permissions`).

---

Declare one of the lenses Graview ships — a calendar, a status board, a coverage, a timeline, a board, a plan, a blocks place — as a titled place with its bindings and options, and read what graview check and add-lens refuse (an option the lens does not take, a lens that cannot draw, a title taken) rather than drawing a lens that quietly ignores a key.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-shipped-lens.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-sight.html

# graview-sight

`graview-sight` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Say who sees which records of a Graview app, and which of their fields — so a seat is served only what it may see, on every surface at once — verified by graview check and by comparing what a seat is told with a hidden value and without one.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Say who sees what

A grant says who may DO an act; a sight says who may SEE a record, and which of its fields. It is the same kind of declaration — once, in the policy — and the store is what enforces it: every surface a seat reads (the scene, the pages, Find, the log, an agent's tools, the wire) is handed the seat's view, `store.seenBy(principal)`, so none of them has to remember.

### Do this

1. **Say it for every kind.** `sees` keeps records from seats the way grants keep acts: once there is one sight, a kind no sight names is seen by nobody but the system (`sight-unnamed-kind` says which).

```ts sees: [ { roles: "*", kinds: ["car"] }, // the shop window { roles: ["shopper"], kinds: ["test-drive"], own: true }, // theirs, joined to theirs, or made by them { roles: ["participant"], kinds: ["match"], via: "givenBy" }, // only what that relation joins to their own record ] ```

A served store sends a seat only what it sees, withholds the rest of the log in place, and refuses an act that names a record it may not see exactly as one that names nothing — a document's `setsOther` target too; an act's `setsLinked` reaches only the linked records the seat sees, and is refused, naming the record, where one of them is not the seat's to change. A record whose required reference names a kind its seat may not see is withheld whole (`sight-hides-required-ref`): let the role see the target, or make the field optional.

1. **Hide a field, not only a kind.** A roster where parents see every player's name and not their phone number:

```ts sees: [ { roles: ["coach"], kinds: ["player"] }, { roles: ["parent"], kinds: ["player"], hide: ["phone", "medical"] }, { roles: ["parent"], kinds: ["player"], own: true }, // their own child, whole ] ```

`hide` keeps those fields; `fields: ["name"]` is an allow list, so a field added tomorrow is kept until a sight shows it. SIGHTS ADD UP: a field is shown when any sight that shows the seat the record shows it, so the `own` sight gives a parent their own child's phone back, and a person with two roles sees what either shows. A kept field is not in anything the seat is served — the record, the log (an op that wrote it, or whose sentence read it, is withheld), a search, a name, a form, an import — and the seat may not write it: the act is refused as one given an argument it does not take, whatever the field held. A computed field and a rule are worked out over what the seat is served, so to a parent a phone it may not see reads as none.

1. **Load the judge where the store is.** Field sight is `@graview/core/field-sight`: `@graview/ship`'s server entry loads it. A page that holds the whole store (`openStore` from `@graview/ship/browser`, or a `Store` of its own) imports it once — `import "@graview/core/field-sight";`, as `apps/gauntlet/src/main.tsx` does — and so does a host that serves seats without `@graview/ship`. Without it a sight with `hide` or `fields` shows nothing: the store keeps the record rather than serve a field it cannot judge. A page `openRemote` opened needs nothing: its host judged what it was sent, and that store alone is trusted — a whole store on the same page still needs the import. An agent's tool for an act lists no argument writing a field the seat never sees.

1. **Edit it as a document.** `add-sight` and `remove-sight` take `hide` and `fields` like any other key; a field none of the sight's kinds has is refused (`sight-field`).

1. **A notification is a read too.** "Notify me" (`@graview/core/subscriptions`) judges each commit as the subscriber's seat: a change to a record they cannot see never matches, a field kept from them is neither said in the match nor read by its condition, and a change withheld from them says "Someone". Prove it as above: `matchSubscriptions(store, ops, [sub])` for a world with the hidden record answers `[]` (`packages/core/tests/unit/a-subscription-is-told-what-its-subscriber-may-see.test.ts`).

1. **What a seat reads beside a record keeps to its sight too.** - An id is served wherever its record is, so it is never minted from a field some sight keeps from a role: a tip whose title the public may not see is `tip:tip-2`, not `tip:secret-merger-plan` — an act, an import, and a day of a series changed apart alike. An act of your own gets the same from `freshId(name, kind, record?)` when the name quotes an argument for such a field, or a field of the record handed third; a name it builds from anything else is yours to keep clean. - A record withheld whole — its required reference names a kind the seat may not see — is refused as one that is not there, whatever the grant says, exactly as an id that names nothing. - The app's own actor's suggestions say why in words that quote fields; a seat whose sight keeps one the basis read is served the suggestion, and the change it made, withheld. - A sight with `hide` or `fields` shows a kind in part, so even a `roles: "*"` one is not total sight for a worker view: the view's own acts need a press the host saw.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
pnpm build && npx graview check ./dist/domain/app.js
```

- `sight-names-an-unknown-field` (an error): a `hide` or `fields` naming a field none of the sight's kinds has — it keeps or shows nothing.
- `sight-hides-a-required-field` (an error): a role may not see a field every record needs, so it is shown no such record at all.
- `sight-hides-a-labeled-field` (a warning): a kind's label or description reads a field some role may not see; that role is told the name worked out without it.
- `act-reads-hidden-kind` (a warning): an act a role may run reads a kind that role may not see — its condition, its refusal, a value it sets, or what a TypeScript act declares it `reads`. Let the role see the kind, keep the act from it, or read only what it sees.
- `rule-says-hidden-fact` (a warning): a rule's message says a fact over a kind some role told of it may not see in full. A seat's problems are judged over what it sees.

**And try it.** The test that matters is a world with the hidden value and the same world with another, or none — everything the seat reads must be the same:

```ts
const told = (store: Store<AnySchema>) => JSON.stringify({
  snapshot: store.seenBy(parent).snapshot(),
  log: store.seenBy(parent).log.all(),
  problems: store.seenBy(parent).violations(),
  found: search(store, "555", { principal: parent }).hits,
});
expect(told(world("555 0101"))).toBe(told(world(undefined)));
```

### Worked examples

- `packages/core/tests/unit/a-sight-can-hide-a-field.test.ts` and `packages/core/tests/support/hidden-phones.ts` — the roster, world with and without a phone number, every read compared
- `packages/core/tests/unit/an-act-runs-under-its-callers-sight.test.ts` — a hidden record, the same comparison for an act's answer
- `apps/gauntlet/src/domain/policy.ts` — staff kept from the visitor, and where a speaker comes from kept from them too
- `packages/core/tests/document/fixtures/secret-santa.gdd.json` — a sight via a relation

### What the check cannot see

- Whether a TypeScript act's `describe` reads a hidden field directly: the store withholds such an op from the seat as it runs, but the author is the one who knows it was meant.
- Whether what a seat may not see is what the people involved expect. That is a conversation, not a declaration.

---

Say who sees which records of a Graview app, and which of their fields — so a seat is served only what it may see, on every surface at once — verified by graview check and by comparing what a seat is told with a hidden value and without one.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-sight.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-studio.html

# graview-studio

`graview-studio` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Open an app's declaration as a graph in Graview's own interface, change it with ordinary acts, let graview check judge the result before it is applied, migrate a stored graph, and write the declaration back as the files graview create writes.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Work the declaration in the studio

The declaration — kinds, fields, edges, acts, rules, roles, grants, lenses, brand — is itself a graph. `@graview/studio` declares that graph with the same `defineNode` an app uses, so a change to the declaration is an act with an author, an intent and an inverse, judged by the same checker, undone like any other.

### Do this

1. **Open the studio over the app**, in a test, a script or a page:

```ts import { createStudio, createStudioLens } from "@graview/studio"; const studio = createStudio(app); // the declaration, as a store ```

The store's nodes have stable ids: `declared:plot` (not `kind:plot`, which is the layout's name for the district), `field:plot.label`, `edge:plot.tended-by`, `act:tend`, `rule:every-plot-tended`, `role:coordinator`, `grant:2`, `lens:coverage`, `brand`.

1. **Change it with acts**, not by hand:

```ts studio.store.apply({ name: "add-field", args: { kind: "declared:plot", label: "soil", type: "enum", required: true, options: ["clay", "loam"] } }, { author: june, intent: "Plots have soil" }); studio.store.apply({ name: "add-act", args: { kind: "declared:plot", label: "resize", title: "Resize", writes: ["size"] } }); studio.store.apply({ name: "add-rule", args: { kind: "declared:plot", label: "sized", description: "A plot has a size." } }); studio.store.apply({ name: "name-repair", args: { rule: "rule:sized", act: "act:resize" } }); ```

The acts: `add-kind`, `rename-kind`, `remove-kind`, `add-field`, `rename-field`, `remove-field`, `retype-field`, `set-required`, `set-options`, `describe-field` (a field changed in place: `{ id: "field:vendor.notes", type: "string" }`), `add-edge`, and to another app's kind `{ name: "add-edge-to-another-app", args: { kind, label, to: "@nick/house/house" } }`, `remove-edge`, `add-act`, `remove-act`, `add-rule`, `remove-rule`, `name-repair`, `forget-repair`, `add-role`, `grant`, `revoke-grant`, and the derived `edit-<kind>` for what no act names (an inverse, a title, a lifecycle).

1. **Check before you apply.** `studio.check()` is `graview check` on the declaration as it now stands. `studio.apply()` refuses while there are errors and says which; otherwise it hands back `{ app, migration }` — the migration is `null` when a stored graph needs nothing, else a `{ from, to, title, apply }` to append to the app's migrations (the new app already carries it and the bumped version).

**Opened on a document** (`createStudio(compileDocument(d).app)`, with `compileDocument` from `@graview/core/check`), the studio hands back a document, not TypeScript. `studio.edits()` is the change as `editDocument`'s own ops (`add-field`, `rename-field`, `set-required`, `set-options`, `add-relation`, `remove-act`, `add-rule`, and a grant, a sight or the people kind as `add-grant`, `remove-grant`, `add-sight`, `remove-sight` and `set-people` …); `studio.document()` is the opened document with them applied, every act, label, brand and money field untouched. `check()`, `would()` and `apply()` judge by compiling that document, and `apply()` hands back `document` with `app` compiled from it. A copied app, or one with its policy swapped, says it: `createStudio(app, { document })`; without one, `whyNoDocument()` says why. A change no op says yet — a relation's cardinality, a lifecycle, a role, retyping a money field — comes back as `documentFindings`, one sentence each, and no document. Ask ahead what it keeps but will not change: `uneditable(document)` is one note per format, unit or list item type (`kinds.vendor.fields.quote`).

Without the studio, `editDocument` covers the rest of a document too: `add-lens` (`replace` retitles; `at` puts one back), `remove-lens`, `{ op: "set-lens-hidden" }` (`hidden: true` keeps a lens off the bar and the page list, still reached by its address, a link or `navigate`), `set-home`, `arrange-pages` (`order`, `hide`, `first`, `scene` and `pages` — the switch's words; `null` clears), `set-computed` (`expr: null` removes it and what reads it), `set-format` (a number's `format` — `money`, `percent`, `duration` — and `unit`, or a text field's `markdown`; `null` clears; said in words, "money in USD — 10000 reads $10,000"), and `set-view` for a kind's slot, `slot: "home"`, or `lens: "<title>"`. Blocks are checked as they are set. A rename reaches lenses, the home, pages and computed expressions through the parser; removing a field or relation a lens draws by is refused, naming the lens. Computed fields are studio nodes, kept on hand-back and written-back TypeScript.

1. **Write it back.** `studio.files({ schemaVar: "gardenSchema" })` is `src/domain/schema.ts`, `mutations.ts`, `invariants.ts` and, with roles, `policy.ts` — the files `graview create` writes. Shape is what a graph carries: an act the studio declared gets a body from what it says (create, connect, sever, write); an act the checkout wrote keeps the checkout's body under the studio's declaration; a rule the studio declared judges nothing until the checkout gives it an `evaluate`. Read the files before you commit them, and keep a hand-written body where the comment says so.

1. **Let an agent propose.** `studio.propose(call, agentPrincipal, intent)` applies under the agent's seat in a batch of its own; `studio.proposals()` lists what stands; `studio.decline(batchId)` undoes one; accepting is applying. In the interface, the trail shows the agent's turn with its undo, like any turn.

1. **Put it on a page.** The studio is an app: mount `studioApp()` with `declarationToGraph(app)` as the seed, and register `createStudioLens(app).View` over `kind` with a title — a place, "What the checker says", one press from anywhere.

### Then find out whether it worked

Run `graview check` on the app the studio applied, and the checkout's own verify on the files it wrote. Say what they said.

### What the check cannot see

- Whether a body the studio wrote does what the person meant. It does what the act declares — create, connect, sever, write — and nothing more.
- Whether a rule the studio declared is right. It judges nothing until the checkout gives it an `evaluate`; the checker sees a rule, not a judgment.
- Whether a migration is safe for data it has not met. It is computed against the stored graph when it runs; look at the primitives on a copy.
- Whether the files should replace the checkout's. Read them; a hand-written body is the checkout's to keep.

---

Open an app's declaration as a graph in Graview's own interface, change it with ordinary acts, let graview check judge the result before it is applied, migrate a stored graph, and write the declaration back as the files graview create writes.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-studio.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-sync.html

# graview-sync

`graview-sync` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Keep a Graview app in step with another system — a graph projected from it as a snapshot, a SyncEngine that sends this app's acts back and holds a field both sides changed, a remote that speaks MCP behind a door on the dev server, and a Google calendar or a Notion database declared as a connection — and verify the first run sends nothing and a conflict is held rather than assuming the two agree.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Keep an app in step with another system

Often the records already live somewhere: a tracker, an analysis, a calendar. The app is then a projection of them that people act on, and every act has to reach the system that owns the record — or be refused, in a sentence, where that system owns it. Storing, migrating, serving and exporting the app itself is `graview-ship`.

### Do this

1. **Project the other system as a snapshot.** Write the projection with `writeSnapshot(graph)` from `@graview/core/snapshot`: a header line (`generatedAt`, records per kind, links per kind, where each kind's lines are), then a record per line. `readSnapshot(text, { kinds })` parses only those kinds, and `fetchSnapshot(url, { kinds })` fetches only their bytes; an old `{ nodes, edges }` file still reads, and `--seed` takes either. Open it with `openStore({ seed, storeOptions: { principal: rememberedPrincipal() } })` so the page's acts are its reader's.

1. **Sync back with `SyncEngine`** from `@graview/core/sync`:

```ts const sync = new SyncEngine({ store, remote, applyInbound, conflicts: "report", mapping: { system: "n-dx", resources: [ { kind: "task", resource: "task", fields: { status: "status" }, version: "lastModified" }, { kind: "zone", resource: "zone", fields: {}, readonly: true, because: "Sourcevision owns the zones." }, ] } }); sync.guard(); // an act on a zone is not offered, and refused, with that sentence ```

`version` links every projected record at the version it was made from, so the first run sends nothing. `report` holds a field both sides changed and sends neither until `resolve`; `theirs` lands theirs through `applyInbound`; `ours` sends ours — `report.resolved` says which it took. A refused delete is said once; one made there goes through `removeInbound`, or, without it, stays here unsynced (`report.gone`).

1. **A remote that speaks MCP** is `mcpRemote({ call, pull, push })`: `call` is `mcpClient({ url, allow })` in Node, or `doorClient()` in a page behind `mcpDoor({ call, allow, admit: fromThisApp })` on the dev server (`fromThisApp`, `openDoors` from `@graview/ship/dev`) — the door holds the token, takes only JSON from its own origin on this machine (`hosts` names others), from the page opened at the address the dev server printed, and only the allowed tools. It knows no seat: never put it where sight is a boundary.

1. **Keep it in step with a Google calendar by declaring it.** A document's `connections.<name>`: `system: "google-calendar"`, `calendar` (or `{ env }`), `kind`, `fields` (`summary`, `start`, `end`, `location`, `description`; a `date` field is an all-day day; one with `repeats: true` is a recurring event, its repeat the RRULE and each day set apart an EXDATE, kept as a wall time in `brand.timeZone`; with `days` — an enum of weekdays or a list holding `mon`…`sun` — the record is weekly and `start`/`end` are `"HH:MM"` strings there, one event with a weekly rule from the week it is first sent; a one-off or one week's exception in Google is not a record here), `filter` (`{ color: "Basil" }` or `{ tag: "#graview", keep? }`, absent for all), `direction` (`"read"` refuses acts on the kind; `"both"`), `conflicts`, `every`, `paused`. `serve` and `preview` run it with `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`/`_CLIENT_SECRET`/`_REFRESH_TOKEN` (or `auth: { env, file }`), the cursor in `connections.json` beside the data; `--no-sync` leaves it off. A host calls `runConnections({ app, store, state, token })`.

1. **Keep it in step with a Notion database by declaring it.** `system: "notion"`, `database` (its 32-character id, or `{ env }`), `source` when the database holds several data sources (one's name or id; refused otherwise with a sentence naming them), `kind`, `properties` (field → property name, or `{ name, type }` for the checker to judge the type; absent, each field finds the property of its name and the name field the title), `direction`, `conflicts`, `every`, `paused`. The secret is an internal integration's, read from `NOTION_TOKEN` (`<auth.env>_TOKEN`) or handed by the host's `token`; share the database with the integration. Title and rich text, number, select and status (an `enum`), multi-select (a `list`), date (`date` or `datetime`), checkbox, URL, email and phone go both ways; people are read as names; formulas, rollups and files are left alone and said once. A page archived there is gone here, and one removed here is archived there. `scriptedNotion()` is a Notion in memory to test against.

What a change there lands through, credited to the system: a page or event made there becomes a record through `add-<kind>`, or else the first act that creates the kind with no `on` and requires only mapped fields — never one that logs it on another record. When none fits, `connection-creates` says so in the person's words ("Blocks need a Type, and Google events don't have one.") with `fixes` a host offers as buttons — a default, the field left blank, an event part mapped, another kind, a kind made for events — each with its edits (`set-default`, `set-required`, `set-connection`, `add-kind`) where one can be written, and the framework's own sentence as `details`; a change lands through the derived `edit-<kind>`, which writes every mapped field even where a named step (a status moved along) writes it too, so declare no `edit-<kind>` of your own unless it writes them all (`connection-edit`). One this store refuses (a blank row) is said once, kept as `skipped`, and tried again when it changes there.

1. **Several Notion tables joined by relations: one connection per table, relations as edges.** Declare the edge on the kind (`"reindeer": { "to": ["reindeer"], "cardinality": "one" }`) and map it to the relation property in `properties` (`"reindeer": "Reindeer Fleet"`, or `{ "name", "type": "relation" }`); the kind it reaches must be another Notion connection's. A link in Notion lands through `connect-<kind>-<edge>` / `disconnect-…`; one made here is written as the whole relation. A page not read yet is held and linked once its table is, whatever order the connections run in (`runConnections` shares one `sharedLinks()`; a host making engines itself passes one `links` to every `connection()`). A relation of one keeps the first page and says the rest once. For a dual relation, declare the edge on the side you need; declaring both sides converges with nothing sent. A read-only connection refuses links made here. An edge both sides changed is a conflict like a field, under `conflicts`.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
npx graview check --document app.json
```

`graview check` judges a connection before anything is sent: a kind or a field it does not have (`connection-kind`, `connection-field`), a field of the wrong type for the event's part, a start and an end that are not both days or both moments (`connection-when`), a filter it cannot read (`connection-filter`, `connection-color`, `connection-tag`), and it warns `connection-remove` when no act removes the kind, so an event deleted in the calendar would stay here. For Notion it refuses a secret written in the declaration (`connection-secret`), a field that cannot hold the property's type, a relation property mapped to a field or another type mapped to an edge (`connection-relation`), and an edge to a kind no Notion connection keeps (`connection-relation-target`); it warns a people property is only read (`connection-read-only`). Report what it said; a host's line says why it could not reach the other side (`report.problem`).

Then run the engine against a scripted remote in a test: the first run after a projection sends nothing; a field changed on both sides is in the report and sent by neither until `resolve`; an act on a read-only kind is not offered and is refused with its `because`. Against Google itself, `node scripts/verify-google-calendar.mjs` (credentials of your own, never in CI) writes its claims to `docs/google-calendar.json` — a round trip both ways, an all-day event kept a day, a declared filter honored — and `node scripts/verify-notion.mjs` does the same against a Notion workspace (`docs/notion.json`; `--stub` against the scripted one).

### What the check cannot see

- Whether the mapping is the right one: a field mapped to the wrong field on the far side syncs faithfully and wrongly. Change one record on each side by hand and read both.
- Whether `theirs` or `ours` is the policy the people on both sides would choose. `report` is the one that asks them.
- Whether the door's `allow` is narrow enough. It is the token's reach on this machine; name the tools the sync calls and no others.

---

Keep a Graview app in step with another system — a graph projected from it as a snapshot, a SyncEngine that sends this app's acts back and holds a field both sides changed, a remote that speaks MCP behind a door on the dev server, and a Google calendar or a Notion database declared as a connection — and verify the first run sends nothing and a conflict is held rather than assuming the two agree.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-sync.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-tidying.html

# graview-tidying

`graview-tidying` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Tidy a Graview app without losing anything — set records aside (archive, bring back) instead of deleting them, merge a duplicate into the one that stays, and let the app's own actor link and prune by suggestion a person accepts or declines, held to what people said, and suggest changes to the app itself learned from how several people use it — verified with graview check and by undoing it rather than assuming nothing was lost.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Tidy without losing anything

A list that grows fills with what is finished and what was entered twice, and the only tidy a bare store offers is a delete, which takes the record's links and its history with it. Every kind can already set a record aside and fold a duplicate into the one that stays, and an actor that tidies on its own can be told what it may not touch. What a list offers, the order it opens in and how its cards read are `graview-lists`.

### Do this

1. **Set records aside instead of deleting them.** Every kind has `archive-<kind>` and `unarchive-<kind>` (`{ id }`, "Bring it back") and `merge-<kind>` (`{ id, into }`: `into` takes the duplicate's links and the duplicate is archived), permitted through the acts that create the kind. An archived record is out of lists, the scene, counts, computed fields and rules; its own page and search still find it, marked. A list says "+3 archived" and opens them at `?archived=true`; a rule reads them with `all('feature', true)` (`'all'` for both) and `archived()`. A kind that should never be archived says `archives: false` in `defineNode` (a document's `"archives": false`; the edit `set-archives`): it is given no archive, unarchive or merge, and its records are kept or removed. An archived record keeps its fields, its links and its history.

1. **Let the app's own actor tidy, and say what it may not.** An actor that links and prunes on its own is an author that says `automated: true` (`kind: "system"` or `"agent"`). What it is sure of it applies with `lineage: { basis, confidence }`; what it is not it suggests: `suggest(store, calls, { author, lineage })` (from `@graview/core/tidying`) keeps the calls in the log, changes nothing, and they wait in the Suggested tray beside Activity until a person accepts (`acceptSuggestion`, made as them) or declines them (`declineSuggestion`); `declined(store, calls)` says so, and the actor is refused the same change again — matched by what it means (`meaningKey`): the same link by any act that makes the relation, a record made again under a new id, a merged pair either way round. Its run of changes is one Activity row, "Tidied 6 things overnight". Give a night's work one `lineage.run`, name the judge in `lineage.actor` and the records it rests on in `lineage.evidence`; give a suggestion an `expiresAt`, after which it leaves the tray and the next run judges it again. "Not now" is not a decline: it is the person's own state (`Dismissal`, handed to `suggestions(store, who, { dismissed })`), hides it from them alone and binds the actor to nothing. The tray's Not now keeps it in the host's `dismissals`, else the browser; a seat says it with `withNotNow(runtime, dismissals)`.

1. **Hold it to what people said.** A person says "Leave this one alone" on a record (`leave-alone-<kind>`, cleared by `allow-tidying-<kind>`; `isLeftAlone(store, id)`), and the declaration says a kind is never tidied or never linked — `tidying: "never" | "no-links"` on `defineNode`, `tidying: "never"` on a relation; in a document the edit `{"op": "set-tidying", "kind": "vendor", "tidying": "no-links"}` (with `"relation"` for one relation, `"allowed"` to undo it). The store refuses the actor each in a sentence; a person is never refused by them.

1. **Let it dream.** `dream(store, { now, limit, ai })` from `@graview/tools/tidy` runs the actor once. Code puts forward near-duplicates, the records a relation might mean, finished records and empty choices; the host's System One model (`ai.fast`, Jev) does the judging, one request per candidate; code routes each answer by how much the change would undo (`BANDS`) — made, suggested with its basis ("Jev: 0.93 that …"), or dropped. Without a model, or when it fails or the budget runs out, the floor is the judges' own rules: a shared name or email, a link the record's text names, a finished record unchanged for 30 days. It skips what was declined, what waits, what is left alone or changed in the last day, and applies nothing unless the host passes `applyAtLeast`. A host's schedule runs it (`graview dream <entry> --data ./data --model jev-latest --cache ./cache.json`), or reaches the store as the actor through `suggest_changes`, the tool only an `automated` seat is offered. `whileAway(store, { seq }, principal, { dismissed })` is the tray's line, less what the reader said "not now" to; a host that works it out after the first draw hands it over with `handle.setWhileAway(away)` (a React host changes the prop).

1. **Let it learn the app from use.** `learnFromUse({ document, friction, log, records, declined, opens })` from `@graview/core/learn` suggests changes to the declaration itself, each resting on at least `minPeople` (3) distinct people: another word for a kind or a field people searched with and found nothing (`add-alias`; a kind's or field's `aliases`, which search finds and a model is told), a text field whose values repeat retyped to a choice, a date field beside dates written into words (nothing is moved), one act for two people take one after the other (only document acts that set fields), a clearer description for an act agents call wrongly, and a place a host's `opens` counts say nobody opens. It changes nothing: `acceptAppSuggestion` applies the edits through `editDocument` with `lineage: { basis, suggestion: key }`, and `declineAppSuggestion` is kept (`learned.json` beside the store) and handed back as `declined`, never offered again. `graview learn <entry> --data ./data` prints them; `--accept <key>` or `--decline <key>`.

### Then find out whether it worked

```sh
graview check src/domain/app.ts
npx graview check --document app.json   # a document
```

Report **the actual output**. In a document it warns `tidying-redundant` where a relation says `"never"` that its kind's own `tidying` already says, and refuses an alias another kind or field is already called (`alias-taken`). The rest is behavior, so try it:

- Archive one record by its act and ask `graview describe <entry> --place <slug>` again: it is gone from the list and the count, and `?archived=true` finds it. Bring it back; its links are still there.
- Merge two records and undo the merge: both come back with their links.
- Have a test actor (`automated: true`) suggest a link and decline it from the tray: `suggest(store, …)` of the same calls then refuses, and a record left alone refuses the actor's change by name.
- Run `graview dream` twice: the second run suggests nothing new, and its JSON says each finding is already waiting.
- Run `graview learn` after `--decline <key>`: that suggestion is gone, and one person's hundred searches never make one.

### What the check cannot see

Whether a rule should still count an archived record: it does not unless it asks with `all(kind, true)`, and a total that should include last season's says so on purpose. Whether the actor's confident changes deserved their confidence — read a day of its Activity row before raising what it applies without asking. And which of two duplicates should stay: `into` is the one you name, so name the one with the history.

---

Tidy a Graview app without losing anything — set records aside (archive, bring back) instead of deleting them, merge a duplicate into the one that stays, and let the app's own actor link and prune by suggestion a person accepts or declines, held to what people said, and suggest changes to the app itself learned from how several people use it — verified with graview check and by undoing it rather than assuming nothing was lost.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-tidying.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-view-drawing.html

# graview-view-drawing

`graview-view-drawing` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Draw in a Graview worker view — the HTML, SVG and CSS the host keeps of it, the app's tokens and brand, the images a view may show (the app's logo, the app's own images, the pictures on records), a record's video the host plays and its full-screen viewer, files a person drops on it — and find out what the host refused rather than assuming it drew.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Drawing in a worker view

A worker view (`graview-worker-view`: its manifest, its global, its writes and its limits) draws by saying markup; the host draws what the open kit keeps of it into a shadow root it owns, and lists the rest. **What it may draw is broad; what it may load is only what the host chose.** Every image it shows is one the host holds, made for it, or lists the origin of.

### What it may draw

HTML's sectioning, headings, text, lists, tables, `details`/`summary`, `button`, `input`, `select`, `textarea`, `label`, `fieldset`, `meter`, `progress` and `img`. SVG's `svg`, `g`, shapes, `path`, `text`, gradients, `clipPath`, `mask`, `marker`, `pattern`, `symbol`, `use href="#id"`, `filter` and its `fe*`. Attributes: `id`, `class`, `style`, `title`, `role`, `aria-*`, `data-*`, and each element's own. CSS for layout, grid, flex, color, type, `mask-image`, `-webkit-text-stroke`, transitions, `@keyframes`, `animation-timeline`, `@media`, `@supports` and `@container`; reduced motion holds motion still. Each `graview.style(css)` adds a sheet after the last (a shared design system's, then the view's own), each judged alone; a sheet given again is not added twice, so say what changes per push in a class or a `style` attribute.

Never drawn: `script`, `iframe`, `object`, `embed`, `link`, `meta`, `base`, `style`, `form`, `video` (place a `graview-video`, below), `canvas`, SVG `image`, `feImage`, `foreignObject` and SMIL; any `srcset` or `on*` attribute; `href` but a link out (`graview-view-links`); `src` on anything but `img`, and on `img` any address but the ones below. In CSS: `url()` except `url(#id)` on `fill`, `stroke`, `clip-path`, `marker` or `filter`; `@import`; `@font-face`; `@property`; `image-set()`, `attr()` and other unlisted functions; `position: fixed`; `:host`. `position: sticky` is kept — a header held in place sticks within the view, whose region is painted contained — and `all` takes its keywords (`all: unset` takes a button's chrome off). What the host leaves out it lists in `refused` (below).

A view never speaks as the app's chrome. `nav`, `header`, `footer`, `aside` and `search` are drawn as `div`, and `output` as `span`, each with what it holds. They lose their landmark or status role, and a selector for them in your stylesheet still matches. A `section` is named only by a heading it draws (`aria-labelledby`). `role` takes no landmark or notice's role (`navigation`, `status`, `alert`, …) but a named `region`.

A control of your own keeps its role and state, and every `aria-*`: `<span role="checkbox" aria-checked="true" tabindex="0">`, `switch`, `aria-pressed`, `aria-expanded` with `aria-controls` naming an id you drew, tabs (`aria-selected`), `slider` (`aria-valuenow`). Hear Space and Enter on `keydown`. A headless run draws them as the page does.

### The app's look

**Draw with the app's tokens**, so light and dark follow the app's own toggle: `var(--graview-panel)`, `--graview-ground`, `--graview-ink`, `--graview-ink-muted`, `--graview-edge`, `--graview-accent`, `--graview-font-body`, `--graview-font-display` (headings, as the app's), `--graview-font-mono`, `--graview-radius`. Presentation attributes do not take `var()`; put paints in the stylesheet (`.bar { fill: var(--graview-accent) }`). For what the view computes, `props.theme` says the same tokens as values, with `scheme`, the app's `name` and its `logo`. A brand change or the app's toggle pushes `theme` again.

### Its box, and the gutter

On Pages a view is drawn in the page's column, which keeps a 20px gutter either side on a phone. Nothing the view draws passes its box: a negative margin is clipped at its edge, not widened. Say `bleed: true` in the manifest and on a phone (680px or less) the box takes the gutter back (on a place too), keeping the safe areas: a hero is the phone's width. At a desk it is the column's width either way.

### The images a view may show

An `img`'s `src` is drawn only when it is one of these; any other address — another site, a path of the app's of your own making — is refused, and said once in the view's console and the host's problems, with the address:

- **A `data:` image** the view holds: PNG, GIF, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, BMP or SVG, at most 512,000 characters as its URL.
- **The app's logo**: `<img src="${props.theme.logo}">`. The host made it from the brand's mark (a `blob:` URL of the page, or a `data:` image where the page's policy refuses `blob:`). Absent when the brand has none.
- **An image the app holds**, by the content address it was stored at: `/graview/assets/<sha256>.<ext>` (what Graview Cloud's `add_image` answers) — or that path under the app's base, or by the page's own address for it, each the same image. It is drawn only where the host says where those live — `asset` on the view's definition, and on a headless run — and refused elsewhere, with a sentence that says so.
- **An `https:` image on an origin the host lists** — `images: { origins: ["https://upload.wikimedia.org"] }` on the view's definition (and on a headless run). The view never chooses an origin: an address is data it can write, so an open list would let it send what it reads anywhere. It is asked for with no referrer. Unlisted, a URL on a record is refused.
- **A picture on a record.** Say `pictures: true` in the manifest, or `{ width: 400 }`, the widest the view draws one in CSS pixels. Each file on a record the view is handed is then `{ name, type, bytes, width, height, caption, src, left }` in its field, never the host's path to it. `src` is the address the host made from the bytes, fetched as the reader and made smaller to `width`, and drawn at any size as long as you use it as handed; it is absent on the first push, and a push follows when it is ready. `left` says why a picture will never come: past one picture's byte budget or the view's, or what the host answered when it was not loaded. A document, and an SVG, has no `src`: show its name, type and size.

```js
const photos = (job.photos || []).map((photo) => photo.src
  ? graview.html`<img data-key="${photo.name}" src="${photo.src}" alt="${photo.caption || photo.name}">`
  : graview.html`<p data-key="${photo.name}">${photo.left || photo.name}</p>`);
```

Without `pictures`, a record's file comes as the record keeps it: its `href` draws only where it is the app's own image (`/graview/assets/…`).

### A record's video, and the full-screen viewer

A view never draws `<video>` or `position: fixed`; it names what it wants and **the host draws it**, from the records the view was shown, for a view whose manifest says `pictures`:

- **`<graview-video data-record="${node.id}" data-field="clip">`** (and `data-index` in a list): the host plays that record's video in it — poster first, the browser's own controls, only its metadata fetched, captions where the value has them. Size the box in your stylesheet (`graview-video { width: 100% }`); nothing inside it is yours to style or hear. The video comes to the view as its facts — `{ name, type, bytes, width, height, caption, duration }` — so draw its length yourself if you like; never a `src`.
- **`<button data-lightbox data-record="${node.id}" data-field="photos" data-index="0">`**: the viewer's press opens the host's full-screen viewer for that picture or video over the app; Escape closes it and the keyboard comes back to the button. Your code cannot open it.

A record the view was not shown, a field with no video, or a view without `pictures` draws nothing, and says why in its console and the host's problems.

### Files a person drops on it

Say which fields files become — `accepts: [{ kind: "moment", field: "photo" }, { kind: "moment", field: "clip" }]` in the manifest — and mark the element: `<section data-drop="moment" data-drop-connect="takenOn:${day.id}">`. **The host owns the drop**: it draws the target while files are dragged over it, says what dropping does, holds each file to the field its type fits and to the host's files, and stores it. On a phone the same element is a tap that opens the picker. It is a target only where this seat may make that kind and the host takes files. A view that does not hear `drop` gets a record of the kind per file, its file on its field, linked as `data-drop-connect` says, in one change one undo takes back. One that does is told once:

```js
graview.on("drop", "[data-drop]", (event) => {
  const day = event.element.getAttribute("data-day");
  // event.files: [{ href, name, type, bytes, width, height, poster, duration, at, field }], never bytes; event.refused: sentences.
  graview.act("add-moment-to-day", event.files.map((file) => ({ id: day, [file.field]: file })));
});
```

`graview.act(name, [args, …])` is several as one change. Hand an act a file only as you were handed it; any other `href` is refused. `data-drop-field` narrows a target to one field. Every event is `{ type, target, element }` and what it carries: `value`/`checked`, `key`, `pressed`, `files`/`refused`.

**Keep a picture in an `image` field**, which holds the uploaded file (what `add_image` stores), never its bytes as words: a `data:` URI in a text field is cut at 20,000 characters, and in the view's source it counts against its size.

### Then find out whether it worked

1. `graview check` the app, and `checkManifest(manifest, store)` from `@graview/guest/host/views`: it says what is wrong with `pictures`.
2. `graview view check view.js --app <app> --manifest manifest.json --seed <seed.json> --roles <role>` says what it drew. Headless, a picture comes with a stand-in `src` (a blank image), so its `<img>` is drawn and judged; only the page shows its pixels. A picture the page would leave out comes with `left`, and the run says it among its problems.
3. Open the place and read the view's `refused` (`WorkerView.refused`, or `graview.refused` in its console): every element, attribute and address the host left out, and why.
4. Toggle the app to dark, and change the brand where you can. Does the view follow, logo and all?
5. As a member who may see fewer records, are the pictures on the records they may not see absent — not merely hidden?

### What the check cannot see

`graview check` judges the declaration, and `refused` judges the markup; neither sees whether the drawing reads. A picture drawn at full width on a phone, an image with no `alt`, a token used for a meaning it does not carry, a chart whose colors fail in dark: only looking at it on both faces, at 390 and on a desk, in both schemes, sees that.

---

Draw in a Graview worker view — the HTML, SVG and CSS the host keeps of it, the app's tokens and brand, the images a view may show (the app's logo, the app's own images, the pictures on records), a record's video the host plays and its full-screen viewer, files a person drops on it — and find out what the host refused rather than assuming it drew.

The page: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-view-drawing.html · Every Graview docs page, for a model: https://graview.dev/llms.txt

---

Source: https://graview.dev/docs/skills/graview-view-forms.html

# graview-view-forms

`graview-view-forms` is one of Graview's 30 authoring skills: instructions an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code or Codex reads before it changes a Graview app. What it teaches: Let a Graview worker view change records — a bound press (data-act), the fields a person types into, a record's own text filled to edit (data-prefill), a field that saves as it is typed (data-save) and the view hearing what became of each act (acted) — and prove a press applies and a field the view filled is refused, rather than assuming the form works.

Installed into a project by `graview skills install .`, and read by whichever assistant is working beside you.

## The skill

## Forms in a worker view

A worker view (`graview-worker-view`: its manifest, its global, its links and its limits) changes records only by asking for the acts its manifest names. **Where every member sees every record, `graview.act(name, args)` applies as given. Anywhere else only a press applies an act** — a person's click on an element with `data-act`, or a field of theirs that saves — because a view's code is never handed what a person types where sight is not total, and so cannot put words in their mouth.

### A press

An element with `data-act` is a press. Its arguments come only from three places: the record it is bound to (`data-record`, on it or on an element around it), the manifest's constants (an `acts` entry with `as` and `constants`), and the fields in its `fieldset`, named for the act's arguments and typed by the person:

```html
<fieldset>
  <input name="summary" placeholder="What it is">
  <button data-act="set-summary" data-record="package:start">Say it</button>
</fieldset>
```

A field the view filled (`value="…"`) is the view's until the person empties it, and a press carrying it is refused. A radio or a select is the person's pick, not their words: its value goes only if it is one the act declares (an enum's option) or a record the view was shown. A view may empty a field after a press. A press on an act the seat may not run there is refused, and the view hears why.

### What can be pressed

Any element with `data-act` is a press, not only a `<button>`: a `<span role="button">`, a `<div>`, a card's badge, an SVG `<g>`. A click on it or on anything inside it presses it, and a phone's tap is a click. One that does not press of itself is given the keyboard (`tabindex="0"`), is a button to assistive technology unless it says another role, is drawn with a pointer and `touch-action: manipulation`, and Enter or Space on it presses it, as on a button. Three things are never pressed, and the check says so: an `<option>` (bind its `select`, with `data-save="change"`), a `<label>` (a press on it presses its field too), and a field to type into or pick from that does not save (a click into it is not a press). Inside a card that opens (`graview-view-links`) a press is its own: it never opens the card.

Draw a `<button data-act>` first: the host resets every button to the words around it at no specificity, so your own class styles it with nothing to undo. On an element bound to an act, `data-record` is always the act's record, never a link: `<button data-act="acknowledge" data-record="threat:7">` acknowledges that threat and goes nowhere. A control you hear yourself with `graview.on("click")` — `role="button"`, `"checkbox"`, `"switch"` or `"tab"`, `aria-pressed`, `aria-expanded` — is given the keyboard where it has none, and Enter or Space on it is heard as the key and then a `click`, with the page not scrolled.

### A record's own text, to edit

To offer a record's own text to edit, let the host fill it: `data-prefill` names the field, and `name` is the same.

```html
<fieldset data-record="deliverable:email">
  <textarea name="draft" data-prefill="draft"></textarea>
  <button data-act="set-draft">Save the draft</button>
</fieldset>
```

The host fills an empty `input` or `textarea` with the record's whole value, line breaks kept, read through the viewer's sight, when an act in the fieldset writes that field of that record and the person may run it there; otherwise it stays empty, so a seat that may not write the field is offered nothing to edit. The person edits it in place, and it goes only back into that field: a press carrying it anywhere else is refused `untyped`. `graview-worker-view`'s `examples/a-record.js` offers "Edit draft" this way.

### A field that saves as it is typed

In a `fieldset data-record`, a field that carries its own act saves with no button:

```html
<textarea name="notes" data-prefill="notes" data-act="save-notes" data-save="input" data-debounce="1500"></textarea>
```
